the commission has already proposed a directive on the coordination of laws on the administrative treatment of credit institutions' reorganisation or winding-up proceedings. the fact that so much time has elapsed has a great deal to do with the gibraltar affair. the purpose of this directive is to ensure that the resolution of a credit institution and its branches is carried out in accordance with the principles of unity and universality. this means that the home country of the credit institution has exclusive competence to handle the administrative aspects of the reorganisation and liquidation of all branches of the credit institution located in eu member states. this applies in all circumstances except in the cases for which an exception is provided for in article 20 of this directive. the directive is therefore not aimed at harmonisation but at ensuring equal treatment of all creditors and a consistent approach across europe. as rapporteur, i can fully agree with the substance of this report. in consultation with the council and the commission, i have tried to make a number of improvements to this report by means of two types of amendments. the first is that the wording of the council's common position was not consistent with the existing insolvency directive and the directive on the winding up and reorganisation of insurance companies which will be voted on in the economic committee next week. this kind of divergence in directives covering the same subject is unacceptable unless there are good reasons for it. as rapporteur, i have had the honour of making the legislation on this very important subject as clear and unambiguous as possible. all our amendments relate to article 20, which deals with the exceptions to the rule. some amendments bring the directive into line with other directives, such as the insolvency directive and the winding-up of insurance companies, as i have just said. those are articles 20 (1) (h) and 20 (2). they are restated in the report by articles 20a to 20d, but in the same terms as in the other two directives. the second type of amendment is to remove a number of exceptions to the main rule. these exceptions were vague and left room for interpretation. the exception could also be broader than the main rule in the case of the regulated market article. however, the articles on regulated markets, retrocession agreements and contractual set-off and debt renewal were included in the common position as such. i was initially in favour of the deletion of these articles. the problem was only that certain parties within the council could not accept the complete abolition of these articles. i have therefore tried to reach agreement with the council and this was achieved last wednesday at the very last moment. the compromise is still to delete the three articles, only to replace them with three new ones. the compromise articles state, in general terms, that the law of the member state in which the contract is established is not affected. furthermore, these articles also make clear that the insolvency law of the home member state of the credit institution concerned is not affected. this means that if you make contracts with a regulated institution, the proceeds from those contracts go to the estate. that is the point, and that was the intention of my original proposal to delete it. everything is now clear and clear, everyone is happy and i am pleased that we have probably avoided a time-consuming conciliation procedure by working intensively together. we are therefore tabled two types of amendments. one concerns the alignment with other directives, the other the abolition of certain exceptions. i very much hope that this legislation, which i think parliament has improved the quality of, will never have to come into force.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i too was surprised that this debate was to be held today. for more than 21 years, as long as i have been in politics, in the house of commons and in the european parliament, i have been interested in the question of frontier workers. i am interested not only because i am confronted on a daily basis with the problems that frontier workers experience when living in one member state and working in another, but also because there is a lot of technology behind it, a lot of technology that has to be updated every year. i am also interested in it because it shows that parliaments, national parliaments in particular, are not doing enough. i am also interested in it because what politics does not seem to be able to solve, a european court of justice does and there are repeated calls for member states to correct mistakes that have been made. that brings me to a comment to the european commission. i have nothing against the european commission. it is the council, in particular, and its members, that are not prepared to give this frontier work a wide berth, and we, as politicians, especially national politicians, are leaving it to the european court of justice. i think that this is no longer possible, i think that it should not be and that we should try with all our might to use all the means at our disposal to change this. what i want in my report, and i thank the colleagues who have contributed to it, and i thank the previous speakers who have worked on it, is four points. first of all, i urge the commission to draw up a directive establishing a border impact assessment. it is a request that has been made to the european commission and to the member states since 1990. we mean by border impact assessment that every time legislation, social, fiscal, public health changes in the member states, an assessment is made at that time of the effects of this on people living in one member state and working in the other. - why? - why? not because you're fixing it, but because you're preventing it, because you're preventing problems from happening. the second request i make to the council is that the improvements in regulation no 1408 be completed very quickly. i think that this dossier has been on the table of the council of ministers, the ministers for social affairs, for two years. there are a number of improvements for frontier bilateral tax treaties that are being concluded, to see if the principles, whereby taxation and social security should go hand in hand for the country of work, are there to avoid problems and to avoid in writing. - the seppänen report did not receive our support for several reasons. the commission and the rapporteur therefore largely limit sustainability in the forestry sector to planting replacement for felling. however, this is not correct. firstly, mr seppänen does not take biodiversity into account in this way, whereas production forests can easily lead to monoculture. so it is necessary to plant a variety of essences. the producer plays an important role in this respect but is often put under pressure by the free market. a limitation of the functioning of the market is therefore necessary. unfortunately, the report pays little attention to this. secondly, the report does not sufficiently emphasise the need to minimise emissions. wood burning is not a sustainable energy source because it releases co2 and other pollutants. there are more sustainable alternatives such as gasification and composting. secondly, the use of wood as a carbon sink to meet the kyoto emission reduction targets is questionable. in fact, combustion must also be considered as a source of carbon. in addition, the rapporteur does not take account of the principle of subsidiarity when he calls for community intervention in the fields of education, technology and resources for the commission. sustainability is a competitive factor of increasing importance both within and outside the european union. it therefore deserves to be stimulated to a greater extent than the rapporteur proposes.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not affected by the oil spills. less public and political interest is given to another form of maritime transport, namely the transport of bulk goods, particularly ores and coal. the consequences of sinking a ship in this category are smaller in terms of pollution, but the number of crew members killed is considerably higher. let us take a closer look at the accidents involving bulk carriers: 146 accidents in the last ten years, 780 sailors drowned. of these bulk carriers, 69% were over 15 years old. there are two main causes of these accidents. firstly, the lack of expertise of the crew and secondly, the physical condition of the ship. the main cause of the accident was a defect in the hull of a bulk carrier caused by damage caused by improper loading or unloading. this problem has been recognised internationally. the international maritime organization, the imo, has issued the bulk loading and unloading code, the blu code. this includes both ship and shore side duties which apply before, during and after loading and unloading. the imo urges all participating countries to apply this blu code to terminals in their countries. the commission, on behalf of the member states, intends to respond to this call with the proposed directive. it aims to incorporate the blu code, with some modifications, into community legislation. the main points of the proposal are, firstly, the appointment of a terminal representative, secondly, the drawing up of a loading and unloading plan and, thirdly, the right of intervention of the competent authorities in the event of a dispute between ship and shore. the commission also proposes to make a quality assurance system for terminals compulsory, as an alternative to the so-called 'ism code' for ships, which is a quality system. the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism considers this commission proposal a step in the right direction. it will not prevent all accidents, since the fatal damage often occurs outside the european union. it is, however, an incentive for the industry to act responsibly and carefully and thus avoid unnecessary damage. the problem, like the sector, is global, and an international solution is therefore essential. we therefore support the inclusion of the blu code in community legislation. the text of the directive should be as close as possible to the blu code to avoid distortions of competition between countries inside and outside the european union. the commission's proposal is not without its flaws, but it is not without its shortcomings. first of all, i would like to point out the need to ensure the safety of the crew in view of the high number of casualties mentioned. some of the points made in the text on this point are appropriate. a second point: the captain carries a lot of responsibility. it is therefore logical that he should be fully informed and that in emergency repairs his judgment should be the basis for whether to leave the ship or not. it is also important that classification agencies receive reports of damage to bulk carriers, since these agencies often have to assess the condition of a ship. that can only be done if they have sufficient information. thirdly, the role of the competent authority, which hears or notices irregularities during loading or unloading. it must then be obliged to interrupt that process in order to ensure the safety of the ship and its crew. fourthly: it is well known that the port state control (psc) capacity in the member states is insufficient. this directive threatens to give the psc authorities additional tasks. the commission must therefore ensure that these tasks are actually carried out. finally, a few comments on amendments nos 14, 13 and 16. we have already seen that we must stick as close as possible to the text of the blu code to avoid distortion of competition and ambiguities. amendment no 14 is totally inconsistent with that and i cannot therefore support it. there has been a lot of unrest about amendment no 13. the vessel data recorder is an instrument for recording travel data. loading and unloading information is not on there. in addition, imo agreements have already been reached on the mandatory use of a navigational data recorder on bulk carriers. the impact of this is to be found in the erika ii package. moreover, if a vdrl is on board a ship, it is the port state control and not the terminal operator that is responsible for monitoring it. this one doesn't have the knowledge either. in short, you will understand that i cannot support amendment no 13 either. i hope that the colleagues will understand the logic of this. amendment no 16 by mr simpson and mr fava is one i cannot support. this imposes requirements on ships from outside the european union that have not been internationally agreed. that's not legally possible. i'm sure they're working on it. i hope that reassures the applicants. mr president, if we adopt this report, in slightly modified form, i believe we will have considerably improved the safety guarantees for bulk carriers and their crews.

- mr president, in the run-up to the debate in parliament on 16 may last year, mr savary showed that modernisation, extension and internationalisation of the railways is something other than the network. in the 19th century, it was the different gauges and types of rails that prevented the railways from functioning as a single european entity. it was not only the individual states but also the competing railway companies that were to blame. the pyrenees are still a frontier within the european union where the change of track gauge is necessary. in the 20th century, electrification and its associated security systems again tore the railway network apart. where the steam locomotive could still pass through the border, it had to be changed from now on due to a difference in the mains voltage of the locomotive. the threats of the 21st century lie in a combination of technological development and competition. until recently, it seemed that magnetic levitation technology would once again create separations in the railway network in germany. in the netherlands, in fact, such a line between amsterdam and lelystad and groningen is still being considered, even though the possibility of it going through bremen and hamburg to berlin has disappeared. as interesting as that technique may be in some ways, in the short term it means mostly one of the rest of the net separated system. the interests of individual companies seeking to make their latest technology profitable must not be allowed to determine this. despite european integration, we are still seeing a continuing disintegration of the railways. international rail service arrangements are becoming increasingly unavailable. rail tickets to distant destinations often have to be purchased outside the country of departure. not so long ago, a passenger train could go directly from cologne to athens, from paris to lisbon or from amsterdam to copenhagen. not anymore, you know. four months ago, the direct night train from stockholm to berlin disappeared. in addition to the technical measures which this report deals with, it is also essential to put an end to this fragmentation of rail transport. the present situation whereby long-distance railways refer passengers to airplanes and freight to lorries must also be put to an end.
- mr president, the majority of the earth's surface is sea. people can't live there, but we're using the sea more and more. not just to sail from one continent to another, but to drill for oil, to extract other minerals, to dump waste, and to generate electricity from tidal power plants. mercury, lead and radioactive waste are reducing animal life and making fish increasingly unfit for human consumption. shallow coastal areas, estuaries and other transitions between fresh and salt water, where fish used to spawn, have been greatly altered by human intervention. the sea has long been viewed as a source of an inexhaustible supply of food. fishing is done with ever larger boats and with ever more perfected techniques to sweep the sea clean. this is happening in the seas bordering europe, but increasingly also further afield, by european ships off the coast of africa. i have already expressed my opposition to treaties which the european union concludes with third world countries in order to empty the sea there too. in the short term, we are finding a solution to the european food problem and in return we are also paying some money to poor countries. in the long run, however, it is certainly not a win-win situation that everyone gets better at. the need for fish continues to grow while stocks continue to decline due to overfishing and pollution. there are still fishermen who believe that the sea remains inexhaustible. last week i heard on dutch television a fisherman interviewed say: the fish always comes, we've seen it all along, and it's in the bible. this kind of certainty, which has seemed true for centuries, will be increasingly lost in the coming time. it is therefore appropriate to designate times and areas when stocks should be restored and when fishing should not be allowed. for the same reason, the fishing quotas should be limited. the rapporteur acknowledges that cod catches in the fishing ports on the east coast of ireland and northern ireland have fallen dramatically over the last ten years. the quantity allowed today is less than a fifth of that at the beginning of the 1990s. the actual catches below the allowable limit were reduced by a quarter. so the sea is empty. the rapporteur, however, wants to extend the exceptional period of less restrictive fishing by six weeks between 22 february and 30 april and criticises the large size of the sea area to be closed by fishing during the spawning season. fishermen groups protest when they are given the impression that government measures are unilateral to the detriment of their country while their colleagues from other countries are allowed to continue emptying the sea. the pressure then arises to weaken measures and allow more exceptions. this threatens to distract attention from the need to limit catches. the short-term disadvantages of any catch limitation are such as to arouse outrage and resistance. however, it is better to close more areas permanently and completely than to let the fish go extinct because of inadequate measures. the same will be true of the north sea.
mr president, the survival of cod is seriously threatened in several european waters. the commission is right to propose measures to protect this species from extinction. but like the emergency measure announced by the commission for the north sea, its measure for the irish sea is also half-hearted. the commission's measures are based mainly on political feasibility and lack the necessary scientific basis. in the case of the north sea emergency measure, a measure has been chosen which particularly affects the dutch fishing fleet. politically, this is feasible, because the dutch fleet is doing well and other member states and fleets are not able to tolerate it. that is why the dutch protest and the alternatives put forward were not well received. the closure of the area does not have a sufficient impact on the recovery of cod. not in the north sea and not in the irish sea. the fisheries will move to open areas where there is potential for spawning and for young cod. if the fishery moves to areas where concentrations of young fish are present, the measure will even hinder the recovery of cod. it is also noteworthy that the north sea emergency measure does not prohibit the directed fishing of cod with standing nets, in which the animals are caught when they are ready to hatch, within the twelve-mile zone and within the codend. increased fishing pressure in the open areas will also damage the stocks of other fish species and soil ecosystems there. the alternative measure proposed by the dutch state secretary for fisheries, on the other hand, offers a much better chance of survival for cod. this plan, a standstill arrangement for all cod-related fleets for a significant number of weeks a year, may still save the cod. and just as important, this plan is supported by both the fisheries biologists and the fisheries industry. the commission does not, however, consider it politically feasible. the result of her emergency measure is that we may soon find cod in only one european water, namely, strong water! unfortunately, in his report, mr nicholson follows the halfhearted approach of the commission. of course, the challenge for the fisheries sector is great, but it will be even greater when there is no cod left. the commission must examine how it can meet the financial needs of the fishermen, and there is no doubt that this will cost the fishermen sacrifices. in order to secure the future, dutch fishermen are prepared to do so and i am convinced that the fishermen of northern ireland are equally prepared. now the commission.

the rapporteur. - commissioner nielson, thank you very much for taking over from your colleague bolkestein. it's a bit of a complicated proposition. so i won't ask you any difficult questions tonight. i think that's a nice touch. on 23 december 1986 the commission's proposal for a directive on the winding-up and reorganisation of insurance undertakings was presented to parliament and adopted. the first reading was adopted by parliament on 14 march 1989. for the next 11 years, the directive sat on the council of ministers' shelf. this was mainly due to two major obstacles: the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. the latter question concerned mainly the relationship between a guarantee fund for the policyholder and his possible preferential position in bankruptcy law. the last question was raised for a while at the last reading, but fortunately we were able to avoid it during the committee procedure in parliament. so now parliament has the formal opportunity of the second reading. this directive has the same objective as the proposal on the winding up and reorganisation of credit institutions, namely the mutual recognition of legislation. this directive guarantees that insurance undertakings are wound up or reorganized in accordance with the principles of unity and universality. this means that the insurance undertaking must be wound up in accordance with the law of the country in which the insurance undertaking has its registered office and by the competent authority there, the so-called 'unitary principle'. this competent authority should then involve all branches and agencies in the european union in the winding-up process, irrespective of the member state in which they are established. that is the universality principle. the directive should ensure equal treatment of creditors. regardless of the country where claims arise, they are always settled in the country of the registered office. this means that creditors all have the same rights and are no longer dependent on the arbitrariness of the country where the claim arises. unlike the second reading of the reorganisation and winding-up of credit institutions, i believe that this directive is much more consistent and well-structured. i therefore recommend to my colleagues that they adopt the council's common position without amendments. and on this valentine's day, i think that is a good, unanimous position for the council, the commission and parliament.

in writing. - (nl) i should like to take this opportunity to explain the reasons for my vote on the ceyhun report, also on behalf of my colleagues mr belder and mr van dam. i voted against the report and against many of the amendments tabled by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs. given the sensitivity of the subject, aid to illegal immigration, a subject which always arouses a lot of emotions, i wish to explain my position. first of all, i would like to say that i am in full support of the acceptance of the statutory refugees as defined in the geneva convention. they must be welcomed and granted asylum in all member states. unfortunately, in this report, the term 'refugee' is used to refer to all those seeking safety in the union, which is confusing. what is an illegal refugee? if that person applies for asylum on arrival in the union, he is not in an illegal situation. the notions of foreigner, refugee, illegal immigrant, asylum seeker, etc. are used in an incoherent way. such a confused application of various concepts is not appropriate in a text of law where, precisely, definitions must be drawn up and the criminal framework defined. i recognize that asylum seekers who are deported often find themselves in a very embarrassing situation. the humanitarian aid provided by churches and organisations is being swallowed up by the failure of member states and the international community to find a workable solution. that is why i sympathize with the request not to punish those organisations which help illegal immigrants. i must, however, be more specific. a problem arises when the decision of an independent judge based on the law is constantly undermined by the subjective judgment of the people offering their help. moreover, what is the definition of 'humanitarian aid'? does this also apply to a non-profit-making association which, for example, is involved in smuggling as many poor russians as possible into a member state because it wants to help them? the dramatic circumstances of illegal immigration are infamous. we need to have strong and harmonised legislation on penalties for human traffickers and a strong but fair asylum policy which discourages illegal immigration. that is why i supported the proposals of the french government.

mr president, there are two elements to this proposal. one element is the fight against human trafficking as part of the great crime. almost everyone agrees that we must do everything possible to combat the systematically organised illegal immigration. too often we read and see the inhumane way in which people's lives are being treated. the example of the dover chinese is too crude. the other element is the right to asylum. people fleeing poverty, misery or war are not to be blamed. what would we do in such circumstances? europe has a long tradition of humanitarian action and it must continue to do so. the balance must therefore be struck between upholding the refugee convention on the one hand and fighting crime on the other. there is another element to this proposal. the question here is not whether or not to impose fines on hauliers. all schengen countries have had such a system in place for many years and are applying it. but non-schengen countries, such as the united kingdom, as the rapporteur has already mentioned, and canada, for example, also have this type of penalty mechanism. the proposal today is only about harmonizing those fines. in conclusion, mr president, the eldr group believes that a better balance must be found between these two elements. that is why we have tabled amendment no 11 by mr watson and mrs ludford, which would make this system of penalties inapplicable to asylum seekers. we hope that this amendment will be accepted and therefore we find the harmonization as a whole acceptable.
the rapporteur. - mr president, i would like to join with what commissioner vitorino has just said, and that is essentially that the member states of the european union are failing to set up a european asylum policy. in 1999 in tampere, the heads of government may have been of good will, but beyond drawing up a wish list, tampere has not done anything. the european commission's 2000 scoreboard, which outlines the measures to be taken, is clearer. but even now it seems that the council of justice ministers will fall short of the objectives set. the same applies to the establishment of a reception system for displaced persons. the draft directive is the third proposal to be submitted to the european parliament, four years after the first one in 1997. the first two proposals have been approved by the european parliament, but the council of ministers cannot take a decision on them. it has never been clear which member states are the problem, because everything is dealt with behind closed doors. the council of ministers is keeping quiet, and that is again the worst of european asylum policy. this is all reprehensible, because what is this all about? this proposal deals with situations such as those in bosnia a few years ago and later in kosovo, situations in which the mass outflow of displaced persons has to be accommodated in the european union, situations in which people are being driven from their homes, in which villages are being burned and in which people are left with nowhere to go. it's hundreds of thousands of people at a time. of course, they must be treated with human dignity. of course, the european member states must share the responsibility fairly by making good agreements. that has not been done satisfactorily in previous cases. and it 's predictable again . the european union is not ready to accept a similar tragedy in macedonia or possibly algeria. president. - the commission has done a good job. the present proposal is better than the previous two. the distribution of responsibility between the member states is now incorporated in the system and cannot be separated from it. this aspect therefore enters into force at the same time as the rest of the scheme. and there are a number of other things which are certainly better than the previous proposals, but which i will not go into here. that's the good news. now, there are a few things that need to be improved. i am thinking first of all of the connection with the refugee convention, and in particular its most important principle, the principle of non-refoulement, the principle that refugees should not be returned without any further consideration. that should be better reflected in the proposal. the council of ministers must be bound by deadlines when it comes to the decision-making process on the introduction of temporary protection for displaced persons, and the european parliament - this too is an old complaint, mr president - must be more closely involved in the decision-making process. the proposal lacks one point: that is the point of responsibility sharing - we used to talk about burden sharing, now we talk about responsibility sharing - between the member states. it is a question of which member state is making what effort to accommodate the large numbers of displaced persons. in the case of bosnia and kosovo, countries such as germany, the netherlands and austria took in many displaced persons, while other member states did too little. the commission is now proposing, first of all, a financial burden sharing based on the refugee fund. i am convinced, mr president, as your rapporteur, that this aspect really needs to be strengthened. firstly, it is a question of implementing the ec treaty, which explicitly states that the council must promote a balance between the efforts of the member states in this field. that word 'balance' means more than the word 'solidarity' which is now in the proposal. first of all, the displaced persons should be distributed among the member states in accordance with the following distribution key: amendments nos 4 and 11 are designed to do that. i hope, of course, that they will be accepted by this house. the provision that member states may refrain from taking in displaced persons should also be deleted. on the contrary, each member state must give a good reason for its proposal, as is stated in amendments nos 31 and 32. mr president, all in all, there is a reasonable proposal on the table which i hope this house can accept.
- mr president, i too would like to thank mr wiebenga for his excellent work. i can tell you that in the netherlands it is very unusual for our groups to agree on refugee policy. although we wholeheartedly support the report in its main lines, my group also now makes some reservations, of which i will mention two. the first concerns article 13 (1), which has been the subject of much discussion. the commission proposes that member states which treat unmarried couples as married couples in their national law should also do so in the case of family reunification. it is not a question of imposing family law as a norm, but of equal treatment in a member state. it is a modest proposal in my view, but it is an important principle. i am therefore disappointed that this is watered down in the report, namely in amendment no 22, which makes this modest proposal look like an empty shell. it now says that member states can reunite unmarried couples. we do not need european agreements for that, because we are already allowed to do so. the commission's proposal is based on solidarity between member states and the generous provision of storage capacity, but there is no stick behind the door. the rapporteur is trying to make the reception system less optional, and i support him in that, but solidarity is not getting any financial support. i am convinced, as is the rapporteur and some others here, that a sharing of financial responsibility at european level is necessary to avoid member states shifting responsibility to each other. i also believe that it is unwise to engage in unnecessary squabbling with people ourselves. article 24 of the refugee fund provides for financial solidarity. but this fund has a maximum of 10 million euros available annually for displaced persons. that's just enough for two tents and a hot water bottle. unless this fund is substantially increased, i fear for the hospitality of europe.

in writing. -{nl) it is true that we cannot accommodate all of humanity in europe and that we cannot solve the world's problems by moving everyone here. but it is also an illusion to believe that we can keep the fortress of europe closed to people who have to or wish to leave the outside world. these people seem to have a lot of money and take a lot of risks to get into europe. we will only change this situation by helping to improve the situation outside europe, for example by not taking cheap raw materials and semi-finished products out of europe and not doing business with oppressive regimes. the introduction of minimum fines undermines the autonomy of member states in the area of criminal law, and the proposal to increase them from eur 3 000 to eur 5 000 only makes things more difficult. the kirkhope proposal only leads to an increase in illegal immigration and an increase in the profits of the mafia. this is what happens when you punish idealistic caregivers and diminish legal access. as i said on 15 february in the ceyhun report on irregular entry, it is foolish to punish the solidarity of action groups and churches with political refugees and victims of war.
in writing. -{nl) i remember the 1950s, when almost everyone thought that the fission of the atom would provide an unlimited amount of clean and safe energy in the future. a number of countries then built nuclear power stations with enthusiasm, and nuclear fission thus provided a large part of the electricity production. since the 1960's, criticism has increased as it has become clear that nuclear power plants can explode and that waste will continue to threaten the environment for a long time. the harrisburg and chernobyl disasters have slowed down the further expansion of atomic energy and some countries have even stopped or are preparing to do so. but even then, we'll be dealing with dangerous radioactive waste for thousands of years. given the risks involved in transporting this waste, the best option is to bury it in the nuclear power stations that are to be closed and not to transport it. action is being taken to stop these transports. the rapporteur shows some understanding of these actions and wishes to limit the dangers but continues to authorize and justify the continuation of such transport. i don't agree with such a choice.
in writing. -{nl) trade liberalization means much more than the abolition of frontiers or the ending of obsolete protectionism. this means that the price of a product becomes more important than all other considerations. whoever can supply the cheapest product wins the market and sweeps out the more expensive producers. with ever-lower transport costs, it is possible to bring in all raw materials and finished products cheaply from anywhere. competition is forced to choose between providing a cheaper product or disappearing. proponents of this mechanism claim that it makes producers inventive and efficient and that the consumer benefits. this is why unlimited competition should be achieved, preferably on a global scale. there are, however, good reasons for allowing higher production costs and for protecting production against cheaper competitors. such reasons are: safety at the workplace, adequate pay for workers, exclusion of child labour, good regional distribution of employment, respect for the environment, avoidance of animal torture, combating unnecessary traffic, provision of useful and desirable services but which do not generate profit in the logic of the market. this is a task for democratically elected authorities, but the wto agreements subject them to the blindness of the market. although i find the rapporteur's proposal inadequate, i will not vote against something which may contribute to slowing down this development.
- mr president, i was very much in favour of the commission's attempt to put an end to the present system of transfers, which in my view has led to absurd waste. that is why, unlike my colleagues, i am disappointed with the outcome of the negotiations that we have now. of course there are good points in the proposal, such as the reimbursement of training costs. i have a question to add to that, because i do not find the commissioner's answer to my previous question satisfactory. i think that the bosman case will be a major obstacle to the payment of training costs, even at the end of a contract, even when a club wants to lose its player. either the compensation is too low and therefore not a real compensation for the training costs, or the compensation becomes very high and conflicts with the bosman ruling, which provides that no compensation may be paid to the club at the end of a contract. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. you must admit that the commission has not succeeded in changing that element. in future it will also be possible for clubs and players to agree in a joint contract to buy-out sums which are not limited and which can rise to the same absurd heights as now. i think you should be honest enough to say that the commission has suffered a heavy defeat on that point and that the core of the present system is preserved. i can see nothing in the fifa proposal other than an embellishment, and in some respects an improvement, of the present system, but the core of that system, the existence of buy-outs, remains.

- mr president, butter, flax, cigarettes and employment agencies are becoming synonymous with fraud in the european union. millions of european money have been wrongly paid out or, as in the case of cigarette smuggling, lost revenue. this is not about fraud within the institutions of the european union, but on the territory of the member states. the rapporteur, mr bösch, rightly points out that the resolution of these serious fraud cases is the test case for the efficiency of olaf. i would also point out that the full resolution of these fraud cases depends on the efforts of the member states concerned. in order to enforce that commitment, the commission should impose sanctions. i therefore think it is perfectly justified that the netherlands should not receive any money from the european social fund for the time being until it has fully clarified the misuse of these funds. what sanctions are actually prompting spain to clarify the flax fraud? companies involved in fraud should be blacklisted so that they are not eligible for european subsidies again. they seem to be logical steps, but not to the commission. the company fléchard is thus becoming part of a european soap opera: is being persecuted! the effectiveness of olaf is jeopardised by a shortage of staff. if the fight against fraud is one of the priorities of president prodi, he and his commission have a duty to resolve quickly the delay in recruiting qualified staff at olaf. in doing so, the commission must avoid any conflict of interest. we cannot allow commissioners who may be involved in flax and butter fraud to influence the appointment of officials who will investigate their role! as the elected representative of the people, this parliament has a monitoring role. unfortunately, the commission has repeatedly obstructed this control. transparency is a vague word for her. clearness is what this parliament wants and to that end it should be empowered to see olaf's reports!
the rapporteur. - mr president, thank you very much for giving me the floor. i am glad that so many colleagues are here to debate this important subject. i understand that a large number of british colleagues met in the bar to prevent me from speaking. it didn't work. but i also want to thank my spanish colleagues from this place: they have behaved very correctly in the matter of procedure and i think that is commendable, because although they do not agree with me on the substance of the matter, they are here. tribute to the spaniards. i cannot, however, have any more respect for my british colleagues, who have tried behind my back, in my own group, to cancel all debates for tonight. mr president, we have been working on this directive since autumn 1998, which will have to adapt the rules on the emission of pollutants from large combustion plants. despite all the opposition from a number of member states and despite all the warnings and protests from some stakeholders in the electricity sector, i think we can amend the original regulation without any problem. the technical possibilities are wide and in many member states of the european union the adapted rules are already prescribed and therefore normal policy. the environmental requirements for large fireplaces in some countries are often stricter because the acidification of our environment has not yet stopped. if we also think of the ozone problem - you know that many of our fellow citizens suffer from respiratory problems, which are caused in part by nitrogen oxides from traffic and from the sector we are talking about today - then it must be almost a priority for everyone in this house to tackle these problems where it is possible to do so in a simple and effective way. the commission's original proposal to amend the 1998 directive was not a great success: the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include the following: in the first reading parliament showed its best side and did what is expected of representatives of the people, namely to give substance to the concern for man, nature and the environment in general. the council's common position was reached with the greatest difficulty. the ep's wish to include existing installations in the directive was granted and the rules were tightened up a bit. the problem - and my spanish colleagues regret this - was that each country had its own exceptions, and if it were up to the council of ministers it would be possible to continue using old, polluting plants which are not up to date with the latest technology. the common position lacked any vision, it was a tangle of wishes for each. in addition to the environmental arguments, i have also given in the explanatory statement other reasons for the need to tighten up the common position: i have also proposed a few economic alternatives in addition to the need to protect public health (ozone smog). economic alternatives, because we want to build an environmental industry in europe. if we compare the council's emission requirements with those already in force in the united states or japan, we do not get the best picture. it is then said that there is no need to impose requirements on combustion plants, because thanks to mrs myller's report we are getting emission ceilings. if we meet the expectations of those who advocate the liberalisation of the energy market, in other words if we do not make demands or allow exceptions to generate electricity from old, polluting plants, then the market mechanism is disrupted and those who neglect the environment are rewarded with a head start thanks to their cheap energy prices. that cannot be the purpose of european environmental legislation.
- the report by mrs oomen-ruijten is a good report. the big boilers, episode two, is also an important report. it's about acidification, it's about classic air pollution and ozone depletion. acidification was a big word in the '80s. that's when it all started. many citizens think that the acidification problem has been solved, but it has not. we still have a long way to go. at the same time, the energy market has been liberalised. that means that it will be more difficult to enforce environmental regulations. for example, in my own country, the netherlands, a belgian company is buying up dutch gas-fired power stations and replacing them with coal-fired power stations. they're many times more polluting and also bad for co2 emissions. that is why we need environmental rules, and strict environmental rules. the committee on the environment has fortunately supported it, but unfortunately the amendments of the committee on the environment will not succeed: i think that the commission has a duty to do so. but we in the green group would like to know who is responsible for that. the green group will support with pain the christian-democratic amendments, which are weaker because they unjustly exclude ammonia. that is an unnecessary concession to their peasant backyard. we shall nevertheless support these amendments, because the greens have also grown up.
- mr president, large combustion plants together account for 63% of sulphur dioxide and 21% of nitrogen oxide emissions in the european union. the environmental benefits of this sector are therefore significant. the rapporteur, mr oomen-ruijten, has made some good proposals in this respect. the council has revised the directive as a whole, but there is ample reason to make a number of further adjustments. firstly, the emission limit values must be adapted to the present technical possibilities. if we consider that waste incineration plants and cement kilns are only allowed to emit 40 mg of sulphur dioxide, i am surprised that emission limits for incineration plants can be as high as 2000 mg. i can imagine that the large combustion plants would be subject to a less stringent regime, but i do not think it would be acceptable to impose 40 times that. with the present state of the art it is well possible to reduce the so2 emission to 100. the values proposed by the environment committee, which range from 1200 to 300 for existing installations, are therefore certainly not too stringent. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's energy policy is not undermined by the current crisis. the amendments we tabled with the green group are aimed at limit values of 400 for small installations and 200 for large installations. secondly, the bizarre exceptions should be deleted. it is unacceptable to allow large old combustion plants to pollute heavily for 2200 hours a year, and to allow emissions to be exceeded if the fuel, such as the highly polluting lignite, is produced in the country. the exceptions for spain and the islands of crete and rhodes are also unacceptable in my view. the liberalisation of the energy market must be based on equal environmental conditions, so the exceptions mentioned must be waived to avoid distortion of competition. the commission has also proposed that the community should provide incentives for the improvement or renewal of old, highly polluting installations, rather than allowing them to continue to cause serious pollution. thirdly, offshore gas turbines must also meet emission requirements. i know that because of the changing composition of the fuel, it is not possible at certain times to meet the strict emission requirements. but if offshore gas turbines are therefore excluded entirely from the scope, any incentive for improvement is removed. in my amendments i have proposed very flexible emission limit values as an alternative. my fourth point concerns the link between this directive and the waste incineration directive. in the case of mixing different fuels, the final emission limit value is calculated differently in both directives. the result does not matter much, but in practice the combination of these two methods of calculation is not only very complicated but also unnecessary. i have proposed an amendment in amendment no 43.
- mr president, the present proposal for a directive on national emission ceilings tackles the main air pollutants. the main points of this directive are therefore to reduce emissions of these substances below critical levels and to reduce their impact. the most important element of this directive, or rather the part of this proposal which has been the subject of the most discussion, is of course the table which sets out the annual emission allowances for each country. what has played a major role in the debate on this is that there was a lot of protest when the 36 countries, including the eu member states, agreed to different and often less stringent standards for the same substances at the un. the first reading therefore called for the european commission's table, which was ambitious, to be replaced by the un's so-called 'göteborg table', which allowed for higher ceilings. i have already indicated at the first reading that the arguments were not strong. the un agreements are always less ambitious because the situations in rich, prosperous and therefore often more polluting countries are difficult to compare with those in developing countries. in addition, there are direct environmental effects of sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds and also, to a lesser extent, ammonia on our own continent. we, the epp group, have joined the european commission's ceiling at first reading. however, we have improved the ammonia table, partly because of the fact that the possibility of dispersal is smaller. the council's compromise proposal on so2, nox and vocs will, in my view, lead to higher emissions. i can only agree with the council's compromise on ammonia. the commissioner knows as well as we do the problems of implementing the nitrates directive: in fact, no member state meets the standards set out in it. the commission's proposals to further reduce the ammonia ceiling are not feasible in my view. i would add that the effects of ammonia emissions are also partly local and that a lower ambition may therefore also be justified. that means that we largely agree with the rapporteur: we support the first eight amendments. we do not support amendment no 9. we support the table on so2, nox and vocs, and we go back to the council's proposal on ammonia. we also have difficulty with the rapporteur's idea that what we want to achieve in 2010 should actually be achieved in 2004. that seems very ambitious to us. i am also pleased that the rapporteur worked very well with him and that the coordination with the work on large combustion plants was excellent. thank you for that.
- president. - i would like to congratulate mrs myller on her excellent report on national emission ceilings. the four pollutants are: for two substances, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxide, an adequate answer can be found in mrs oomen-ruijten's report on large combustion plants. the problem of ammonia must be solved at local and national level. we are actually missing a piece of legislation on volatile organic compounds. the commission has already adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to volatile organic compounds. but for household volatile organic compounds, which are responsible for one third of emissions, such rules still do not exist. that is why i am asking the european commission when it will finally come up with an eu directive on paints. we must move towards water-based paints, and it is time that rules were drawn up in that respect. the gothenburg protocol has been signed by 36 countries. that's where the veto is. the common position is hardly more ambitious than the gothenburg protocol. within europe, the right of veto on environmental legislation has been abolished. if we as the european union are not able to establish substantially stricter environmental standards than the gothenburg protocol, that is a disgrace. tomorrow parliament will have the opportunity to avoid that disgrace. i hope that 314 or more of my colleagues will vote for mrs myller's excellent report.

in writing. -the time when political currents, interest groups and authorities denied the existence of ecological problems is over. yet new cases of environmental pollution are occurring and old cases are not being tackled sufficiently. today's environmental problems are largely the result of secrecy. companies keep quiet about their manufacturing processes and thus about the production of waste that is released into the air, water or soil. transparency could cost them dearly. under pressure from the companies, the public authorities also remain silent on permits and controls. files are being created, but except for the officials who process them, no one knows what's in them. under such circumstances, residents, workers, environmentalists, and disaster relief workers are often unaware of the real dangers. it's only when something bad happens that people get upset and everyone wants to know what caused it. environmental problems can only be truly solved if there is the greatest possible transparency. the korhola proposal is a step in the right direction and is better than the commission proposal, even if it still contains some possibilities for exceptions and confidentiality.
in writing. -the european union raises funds and distributes funds. it is conceivable that such a gigantic, centralized distribution system would be of interest to fraudsters. in the case of distribution, they then endeavour to be among the beneficiaries. some businessmen assume that they are entitled to subsidies from a government that obviously has too much money. this attitude is encouraged by the stories that have been circulating for decades about the creation of huge unsellable stocks of products for which there seems to be no need. these stocks are partly the result of subsidies. it all started 40 years ago with the scrap metal fraud, and it's still going on today. in the case of the rapid growth of flax production in spain and the subsequent destruction of unnecessary stocks by fire, the name of the then minister of agriculture, now a member of the european commission, is even associated with it. only by stopping the unnecessary circulation of money will it be possible to put an end to these frauds. the national and regional authorities can manage and enjoy these funds much better than the european union, which is far away from everyone and gives the impression that it has too much money.

- mr president, i should like to begin by thanking mr sacconi. in any case, he has gone to great lengths to see if a compromise could be found. but now there has been so much deviation from a certain line that the report has become one-sided, and that is not only the fault of mr sacconi but of the whole commission. anyway, thanks for the consult. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. there is a wide range of opinions on pvc and its effects on health and the environment. a number of member states have already taken measures concerning specific aspects of the pvc life cycle. these measures are not uniform and may therefore also have an impact on the internal market. we in the epp group welcome the green paper: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new technologies. pvc is distinguished from other plastics by the high amount of chlorine added, namely 25 to 50%, and also by the many other additives used in pvc. pvc itself is a very good material in terms of its applications - and we would almost forget that in the whole discussion. pure pvc is a hard material, with high mechanical strength, weather resistance, water resistance and chemical resistance. so it's nice, certainly in medical applications, that we have pvc. the environmental and health problems associated with pvc are therefore mainly related to the presence of the additives and the way in which pvc waste is handled. i would like to mention some of these additions. first of all, the softeners. in soft pvc applications, up to 60% plasticizers, usually phthalates, must be added to make the material flexible. phthalates are hardly used in other plastics and thus by far the main use of phthalates is in soft pvc. there is still some debate about the effect of phthalates on living organisms. then a second point: the cadmium. i think that the industry has already made a number of good agreements on cadmium on a voluntary basis. cadmium is being phased out, so the green paper is basically obsolete in that respect. if not, it's lead. lead stabilisers, or more precisely organotin and lead compounds, are the most relevant and the environmental risks are also greater, especially for the lead stabilisers. after the incineration of waste, lead additives from pvc contribute to an undesirable high level of lead in waste incineration plant residues by about 10%, and this calls for a stricter policy on this point as well. i shall then turn to production and incineration in general. as far as production is concerned, industry has made a large number of voluntary agreements to impose very strict limits on the chlorine that can be released. moreover, research has shown that these self-imposed emission limits are very well met. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market. an important aspect of this is the high chlorine content. in incineration plants, there are two sources: on the one hand, there is gft, as we call it in english, which is vegetable, fruit and garden waste, which also contains a large amount of chlorine, and on the other hand, pvc. that means that we must pay very close attention to the waste in these incineration plants and to the possible release of dioxins. the elimination of pvc from waste facilities is therefore important. it is not just the incineration of waste and the resulting emissions that are at stake here. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the waste incineration plant is not affected by the chlorine. so we have to be careful. we want the commission, mr president, to look with industry at how we can make good and clear agreements in the very short term in the context of this self-regulation. the industry is prepared to do that and i ask the commission to look into it.
- mr president, what are we to do with pvc? some people want to make this material look like public enemy number one. we're not getting away with this. the extent to which pvc has environmental or health problems that do not outweigh its benefits remains to be seen. it could be good. pvc has also been shown to have certain advantages as a material: the blood bags are often mentioned. politics need not assess these benefits. we must ask ourselves how we will deal with pvc if it is found that aspects of its use are unsafe or harmful to the environment. what measures are we taking? and what are the consequences of these measures? the green paper is lacking in these areas in our view, particularly because it does not take into account the alternatives to pvc. it is a nebulous debate that is being conducted by proponents and opponents almost like a religious debate. like the rapporteur, mr sacconi, we do not wish to base our choices on the myths presented to us by supporters and opponents, neither of whom have fully convinced us, but on proper research and on useful comparative material. as long as there is no such thing, it is difficult to expect us to legislate. we do not want to ban pvc now, but we do want to be careful about jumping. the precautionary principle calls for it. the fact that the industry itself is already phasing out cadmium stabilizers is a good thing. we think that something similar should be done with lead and organotin. in general, we think that voluntary agreements by industry are positive and that they should be supported by a european legal framework, so that sanctions are created while adhering to what is possible. the risks in the waste phase are great, because we do not get rid of the harmful substances in pvc. one of the few options is reuse, whereby the harmful substances are simply trapped in the product. however, there is so little reuse at present that it hardly contributes to a solution. the industry can still make an extra effort in this area. i would be exaggerating if i said that we are looking forward to the commission's legislative proposals. the present green paper does not provide a sufficient basis for this. there's a lot to be explained first.
- mr president, in the pvc green paper the commission unfortunately does not go much further than describing the situation and the problems encountered, while it hardly proposes any solutions. this clearly shows how difficult and confusing the whole pvc debate is. we are dealing with different points of view, ranging from promoting the pvc industry to banning pvc. pvc is a very important material in our society. it has been incorporated into many products because pvc is cheap and strong and, moreover, lasts a long time. when considering a substitution policy, we must take seriously the ideal properties of pvc, for which there may be no alternatives. the comparative life cycle analysis shall strike a balance between environmental protection and the lifetime of the product. the differences between hard and soft pvc should also be taken into account. the production of pvc is justified if it meets strict emission requirements. the addition of stabilizers, especially heavy metals, is usually not a problem in the use phase, as these additives are safely stored in the structure of the material. the problem with pvc occurs in the waste phase, mainly because of the emissions of heavy metals and chlorine compounds, as well as the large amounts of residues. the resolution hits the nail on the head by calling for a strengthening of the european waste strategy. unfortunately, recycling pvc is difficult to achieve, so incentives are needed. we must start with the simplest, pvc, which is easier to collect in larger quantities. we are talking about the bulk pvc, such as piping systems, pipes, building profiles, window frames, roof tiles and other waste from the construction sector. the recycling of waste is conditional on the elimination of the heavy metal problem and the reduction of emissions. in the case of cadmium, we must give the industry's voluntary agreement a fair chance. the reduction in lead is also commendable, but we must wait for the results of the study before we can ban it. the elimination of organotin compounds is, in my view, premature. the commission therefore concluded that the union industry did not suffer material injury capacity. i hope, mr president, that soon after the european parliament has spoken, the commission's communication promised for this year will be published.

debate makes that abundantly clear. the sending home of the santer commission was the turning point in the financial management of the union. whereas the council has given the same santer commission a blanket discharge, this parliament has indeed taken its responsibility. this has not only increased the political importance of discharge, but at the same time there has been a shift from an accounting approach to one focused on content and effectiveness. the people's representatives must not only check that all the vouchers are there, but also that the tax money has been used for the right purpose and that results have been achieved. we are assisted in this by the european court of auditors. the committee on budgetary control believes, however, that control can be much more effective. to do so, the court of auditors should actually engage in consistent naming and shaming, i.e. publicly denigrating member states that make fun of it. we also want to see a clear quantification of the error rates at national and sectoral level in order to gain a better understanding of the problems of spending. if this is not achieved this year, the court of auditors will at least have to distinguish between major and minor errors by introducing a so-called richter scale of errors. the court of auditors must also realise that it is not itself above the law. it must stop resisting a real audit of itself and it must publish its financial interests on the internet. unfortunately, we have to see time and again that europeans from east to west and from north to south have little confidence in the accounts of the european union. it is the burden of all those who are responsible for the financial control of european expenditure to win back the confidence of the european citizens. this is a condition for the further political success of european integration and can only be regained if we demand maximum openness. europeans want to be sure that their money is being used to the best of its ability and that, where this is not the case, the organisations and member states concerned are really being consulted. there is another institution which feels it is beyond the control of the ep, and that is not the least: the council of ministers, which again did not feel it necessary to appear here today. the council and parliament have agreed, through a so-called 'gentlemen's agreement', not to look at each other's spending. if you don't check up on me, i won't look at you critically. it goes without saying that this does little to restore confidence. as long as it was purely administrative expenditure, this was perhaps somewhat justifiable. but now we see the council taking on more and more operational responsibilities. this not only undermines the commission's position but is also subject to little democratic control. the committee on budgetary control has therefore concluded that the agreement must be upheld. the court of auditors must report on the council's expenditure in the same way as it does on that of the other institutions. the council's stealthy seizure of power without accountability is contrary to all the basic principles of democracy. the budgetary law and the powers of budgetary control have always been powerful weapons for this parliament in closing the various democratic gaps. we have an obligation to our constituents to exercise democratic control wherever possible. the council, in particular, where the democratic gap is the largest and is only likely to widen, cannot fail to have this form of control. this is therefore an important choice, also as a signal from this parliament to other institutions. i can be brief about the committees and agencies. europe is still being built and, like all dynamic processes, is subject to change. it is therefore only logical to examine structures from time to time very critically in view of all the changes. all european institutions must continue to prove their added value. they must be accountable for the proper use of european taxpayers' money. what is their influence on legislation? are they operating effectively? it is of course sad that the discharge of the economic and social committee has been postponed for the fourth consecutive time because of the fraud of non-existent air tickets. we really need to close this chapter now. i have to congratulate the many colleagues who have worked on the discharge on their reports. the committee on budgetary control has, for the most part, acted with restraint and wisdom in granting a discharge to the commission, but with strict conditions attached to it. we are also pressing for reforms in this parliament. only if we subject ourselves to the same stringent requirements that we impose on other institutions will we remain a credible engine of reform.
in writing. for centuries, many people have considered animals to be utilitarian items that could be tortured or abused. objects that were there for pleasure, their traction, to serve as food or to be tested. over time, we become more civilized and friendly towards them, but not yet if it is possible to make money on their backs. in europe, 38 000 animals are used every year to test new components and finished products in the cosmetics industry, after which they are systematically slaughtered. as early as 1993, this parliament decided to ban the sale of cosmetic products tested on animals, but pressure from industry has continually delayed the entry into force of this text. in the meantime, the european commission wants to relax this ban on sale and only ban tests carried out in eu countries, so that products tested on animals elsewhere could still be sold here. the effect of this legislation would be to move testing to other countries. is there nothing that can prevail over keeping production costs at a minimum level, free trade and wto rules? the other side of the coin is bad working conditions, low wages, environmental destruction and increased animal suffering. it is becoming more than urgent to close the european market to imports of all products obtained by unacceptable means. i based my vote on the advice of the eurogroup for animal welfare.

in writing. -(nl) for most of human history, we had to use wood, metal and stone to make our utilitarian objects. for a long time, the discovery of synthetic materials and the development of the chemical industry seemed to open up unknown possibilities. we now know that a number of new materials, which were initially popular with everyone, such as asbestos and polyvinyl chloride, are not good. the negative consequences only become apparent afterwards. the various types of pvc release chlorine after a certain period of time and, even later, phthalates or other plasticizers. to stabilize it, lead or cadmium is used. from the production and during the addition of other components, dangerous substances are released. when reused, other toxic substances are released again and the quality of the product obtained is so far poor. incineration releases chlorine and dioxins. the only solution therefore seems to be to dispose of pvc waste, but even then pollutants are released. both the european commission and the rapporteur rely on voluntary agreements with industry to limit disadvantages. the risk of a ban on imports of pvc whose quality does not meet the requirements of these voluntary agreements is not yet present, because such a measure could be in contradiction with the wto rules. the rapporteur rightly calls for a reduction in the use of pvc and for the search for alternative solutions to be stimulated. i support him in this approach but i think that these proposals are not enough to really solve the problem.

international community to sign the montreal convention in 1999, which made the new comprehensive global liability system a reality. the montreal convention, which is transposed into european law by this regulation, creates a modernised and uniform legal framework. this is a considerable improvement over the current international system. i would like to raise six points tonight. firstly, i support the commission's aim of protecting and informing passengers about their rights in the context of the development of an air passenger charter. the current conditions of carriage in the airline customer service. some airlines have complained to me about the fact that passenger information leads to bureaucratic red tape. you will understand that i do not share their opinion. the cost and effort of informing passengers is considerably less than the effort of airlines in informing potential customers of new services they are offering. secondly, the member states have agreed that the community itself is a signatory to the montreal convention. i regard this as an important step forward in closing the gap in the common transport policy in the union, as it recognises that there is a common competence in the field of international aviation matters. thirdly, there was some concern about the consequences of the case brought by iata before the supreme court in the united kingdom against the uk government over the way it implemented regulation no 2027/97. the court concluded that the regulation remained valid but contained some matters which were incompatible with the obligations which member states had assumed under previous commitments under international conventions. i think that this complaint is no longer valid now that the regulation has been amended and brought fully into line with the new international system of liability. fourthly, in drawing up this report and the 18 amendments which i have recommended to the commission, i have sought the legal advice of various legal experts and experts in order to avoid any legal doubt in the future. at the same time, i have tried to uphold the right of passengers to information. the amendments were adopted unanimously in the committee on transport. they can be broadly divided into three categories. firstly, the improvement of the commission text; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the free movement of goods are applied in the community. in particular, our committee recommends that parliament should include in an annex to the regulation the text of the information form required under article 6 (2). that's new. this will enable airlines to provide this information in a uniform manner. the text summarises the provisions of the regulation in plain language without any legal jargon. once this regulation enters into force - and i hope it will do so by the end of next year - coinciding with the expected entry into force of the montreal convention - all airlines in the european union will be obliged to make this notification form available to their passengers. the text will then be coherent and in understandable language. that is clear to the consumer. nonetheless, airlines from non-eu countries are obliged to produce something similar for the liability scheme they operate. on reflection, i believe that the union has the right - madam president, in this violent euphoria, voting against is treated as a clean-handed policy or aerial cycling, but my group has fundamental objections to a number of points in this proposal and i shall not sweep them under the carpet. my group, the green european free alliance, accepts that there are exceptions to the principle of publicity. for example, a european defence policy would provide certain operational information that should not be on the street. but all documents must be entered in the register and exceptions must be subject to strict criteria, ultimately by the court of justice. that is the procedure for normal documents, but unfortunately special treatment has been agreed for a potentially too large group of particularly sensitive documents, and i hear very little about that here anyway. the classification of documents as 'sensitive' is decided by a select group of officials within the institutions themselves. sensitive documents do not have to be entered in the register and the court cannot review the merits of this decision. if a smart citizen finds out that the document exists, the same officials will decide on the application. and to top it all off, for documents which do contribute to european policy-making but which come from outside, the author has a veto over both the inclusion in the register and the publication of the document. the court must also accept such a veto. the sensitive documents are a black hole in this agreement on the disclosure of information and here the right to information becomes a favor.
