- mr president, the chernobyl disaster was not an exception, so it was not something that was characteristic only of one type of nuclear power plant as those produced and used in the former soviet union. even before 1986 there was the disaster in harrisburg, u.s.a., where an overheated and melting nuclear reactor in the ground was threatening to sink. the point is that there has been too much optimism about the characteristics of nuclear energy all over the world since the 1950s. what was expected was an inexhaustible source of cheap and clean energy, but instead it was a hazardous plant that continues to seriously pollute the environment even after production has been stopped for a long time. fifteen years after the disaster, large areas of belarus and ukraine are still uninhabitable for people who do not want to get cancer. those who stay have become dependent on government aid, and those who should be able to help the most affected people are avoiding or leaving the area. food from the contaminated area remains unfit for consumption. the solution does not require a new type of nuclear power plant, but a systematic rebuilding of the affected area, alternative energy generation and energy saving. it is only in the interests of all europeans to contribute financially to this, otherwise we are organising waste and disasters for the future.
- mr president, in belarus the chernobyl disaster is commemorated every year on 25 april and tens of thousands of people take part in the commemoration. in the west, it is hardly known why, because the nuclear plant was in ukraine. but anyone who studies the consequences of the disaster must note that the consequences in belarus, where more than 70% of the nuclear fallout landed, were at least as bad as in ukraine. in the latter country, nearly two and a half million people were exposed to radioactivity. the ukrainian government has spent $6 billion over the past decade to combat the consequences. there's no end to this spending for a while. to name a few examples: we need money to repair the hull built around the exploded reactor. it's not safe. there 's still a lot of material contaminated by the explosion that needs to be stored and processed . there is still a risk of contamination of ukraine's main river, the dnieper. the european union has faced some of these problems in good time and is providing a lot of support to ukraine - the commissioner has already referred to this - although there are often doubts about the effectiveness of this support. the situation in belarus may be even more serious. there, some two and a half million people still live in contaminated areas where they often eat contaminated food. the health situation is particularly worrying among the children. the socioeconomic situation in that country is bad anyway, which makes people more vulnerable to disease and disability than normal. the government in minsk, while spending a large part of the public budget on the consequences, refuses to deal with the problem openly. its policies are often counterproductive and it shields the problem from the outside world. the international community is involved, but on a small scale. ngos work under difficult conditions. i have particular admiration for the european organizations which take thousands of children on holiday to western europe every year to have them recover somewhat from the effects of radiation. but of course, that is far from enough. the european union has a difficult relationship with the undemocratic regime in belarus. we understand that. at the same time, it is difficult to accept that no further efforts are being made, precisely in the interests of the people affected who have nothing to do with government policy. it has been discussed before, but i would urge the commission once again to allow more targeted aid to belarus. i do not find the argument that neither the tacis programme nor echo allows this convincing. we are talking about hundreds of thousands of people who are still in distress and still in need of immediate help. in this exceptional case, let us overcome our own political and bureaucratic barriers.

in writing. -(nl) the extent to which information is public is not determined by the amount of insignificant or uncontested information available on the internet. it is precisely documents about which authors and buyers can decide to keep the content or even the existence secret. by accepting this proposal, we are still a long way from the concept of access to documents as it exists in the netherlands and scandinavia. the form of restricted access presented here may even be a systematic means of protection against snooping in the case of documents which remain difficult to access by the public. the supporters of the compromise do not seem to be overjoyed either, but nevertheless invite everyone to vote in favour. the main arguments put forward are that the outcome is likely to be worse in the absence of a compromise and that they expect an improvement after the 2004 evaluation. opponents of public access to documents were silent during the debate but without them there would have been no need for difficult negotiations 'behind the scenes' and we could have voted today on a better result. because of this improper and hasty preparation, we now find ourselves in a situation where moderate opponents vote in favour, while radical opponents are forced to vote against the proposal.
in writing. -{nl) four small countries in europe are multilingual, namely belgium, switzerland, moldova and macedonia. in one part of the country, the majority of the inhabitants speak the same or a related language as that of a neighboring country. the same is true of another part, but it is a completely different language. most of the inhabitants find it annoying to be cut off from their neighbours by a border and wonder why they have to remain associated with a region whose language they understand little or not at all. anyone who wishes to preserve the unity of these countries must ensure that there are no second-class citizens, so that no party feels wronged or inferior. this approach is only successful if the population can receive education in the language of the majority in that part of the country and if it is run by people who speak the same language. the macedonian government has not yet understood this, causing despair among some of its citizens. it emphasises the presence of a few albanian ministers but does not ensure collective equality, as is the case in belgium and switzerland. supporting this country financially and promising eu membership can therefore lead to the belief that there is no need to solve the problem and is tantamount to denying the anger of a large part of the population. by giving this hasty support, we are unwittingly calling for violence against the state.

the rapporteur. - madam president, this is the third time we have spoken on this subject and to conclude it the council and parliament have had a very exciting night. it will not surprise anyone that the discussion in our conciliation committee that evening was dominated by the court's ruling on the tobacco advertising directive. there are many legal aspects to this and the question is whether we acted in accordance with the spirit of the court's ruling and that nothing more could be expected of us. the export provision has been agreed so that from 2007 tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide will be subject to the same criteria as products sold within the european union. in that sense, the case has been brought into line with the court's ruling. i am also glad to see that this matter has now been raised in the world health organization. we have reached agreement on the disclosure of ingredients and on the common list of ingredients. a provision of the utmost importance and groundbreaking. before the end of 2002. then there is the subject of misleading descriptions. major cigarette manufacturers, such as philip morris, agree with what parliament and the council wanted to achieve on this way to do so is in shipping, which is partly outside the territorial waters of states. there are attempts to navigate with wrecked ships and underpaid crews. these vessels are registered in a country other than that of the owners, preferably one with low taxes and little control. the crew is recruited where unemployment is high and the remuneration of labour is low. many ships are old and neglected, and there is a high chance that garbage and cargo will end up in the sea. the safety of the personnel is often low and the environmental risks are high. i believe that it should not be ensure that classification societies are not dependent on those whom they are required to monitor, because without such a guarantee any monitoring would be pointless. i am happy to support proposals - mr president, i think i should first of all state, in accordance with our rules of procedure, that i have a double interest in this matter because i am also treasurer of the party of european liberals and democrats. it is not a financial interest, because it is an unpaid position, extremely unpaid, i might say, but nevertheless i think that there is at least a possible political conflict of interest. i am speaking here on behalf of the liberal group and not on behalf of the european liberal democrat and reform party. the first thing to be said in this whole debate is that the situation as it is now is really unacceptable. the situation where the political groups keep the parties afloat. it's been a given. there was no other method of doing this but i think we all understood, even emotionally, that this cannot continue. the court of auditors has indicated that, and that is a good thing. of course, nothing mysterious happened. it's all been done in the open, everyone's seen it happen, but it can't go on like this. now our parties cannot live on the wind, and if they do not receive support from general resources, where will that support come from? we want the european political parties to become the plaything of any interest group, whether it be trade unions or companies or other non-governmental organisations or wealthy individuals or anyone else. it is clear that political parties must be able to exist independently. if we do not, we will have american conditions here and i would like to refer not only to president bush but also to the practice of candidates actually being involved in fund-raising rather than in politics. we must never find ourselves in such a situation. we need parties that work well. mr poettering and mr barón crespo have already said that very eloquently. after all, that's how representative democracy works best. this is true at national level and it is even more so at european level. we need stability in our democracy in view of enlargement. the new countries that come in are also politically active. there are also political parties which must feel at home in the existing european political families. only in this way can we in this parliament help democracy to progress in the future. that is of great importance. we also need this stability for the democratic development of the european union. we do not know how it will develop, but we cannot exclude the possibility that there will be a time when there will be some sort of european lists in elections. then someone will have to put those candidates forward. we cannot exclude the possibility of a system whereby individuals can become members of european political parties. there will also have to be a proper system for that. in addition, those parties need to be independent. it is, of course, a pity that political parties are financially dependent on those who are elected on behalf of that political party. it's got to be the other way around. those who are elected must be controlled by their political parties. that is the way democracy works best and in that respect i think that even the present system can be improved. there's more to say. we are of course very much in agreement that this cannot be seen as support for national parties. we also agree that the system does not mean that pro-european campaigns are financed by it. we think there are a number of issues that need to be addressed, such as legal personality. we have to look further. the issue of support for political campaigns, for example, is yet to be discussed. we can come back to this at the review which will take place in the foreseeable future and then we can perfect the system even further.
in writing. -{nl) parties must be organisations from the bottom up, not from the top down. real parties do not arise because the structures of a state need to organise a competitive struggle in elections but because there are groups of people who share similar ideas, interests and activities. however, the advocates of a european state made up of several peoples have discovered that there is no european public opinion. and now, in an artificial way, from the top, they want to promote leaders and structures that try to create this opinion. four groups of parties with more or less identical ideas in different member states have formed a european party, partly financed by the joint groups of the same parliament. in my view, this proposal is primarily a means of legalising this abuse. the distribution of taxpayer money to parties and the fact that the authorities impose rules on the former reinforce citizens' distrust of what they consider to be a political elite. a centralised european party risks, within a common political movement, the disappearance of the commitment of its members, of party democracy and of the different priorities specific to each member state. although i think the intention of this proposal not to discriminate against parties on the basis of their political sympathies and importance is a positive one - as is the ban on corporate donations, i am voting against it.
in writing. - (nl) it is essential that a democratic europe can rely on european parties. the latter offer the citizen the opportunity to vote directly for a party. the elections, with european lists and list heads, must serve as a basis for the composition of the european commission. a strong legal basis is essential for the creation of european parties worthy of the name. to this end, it is essential to define transparent funding criteria and to guarantee the independence of politicians and parties. we're not for sale. it is unthinkable to accept money from public or private companies, even if it is small. we serve the citizen who elected us. brussels is an attractive place for companies wishing to exert pressure. lobbyists often do useful work by informing us. however, because of the sometimes conflicting interests of the european parliament and the pharmaceutical industry (prices of aids drugs) or the automotive industry (environmental standards), for example, we cannot accept money from them. now that we are in the phase of building european parties, we had better create a single european standard. i therefore call on the greens, the liberals and the christian democrats to support this standard.
in writing. - the cercas report was not approved for the following reasons: first of all, the report makes social security a community tool in the formulation of policies and related measures. the report therefore sets out a vision: the pursuit of social convergence. member states therefore have limited scope to create their own solutions. the diversity of systems requires that each member state develops its own, perfectly adapted approach. many large member states still need to restructure their pension systems due to the ageing of the population. supranational aspects concern related conditions, such as budgetary implications and the requirement that the constitution of pensions in a given member state cannot constitute an obstacle to mobility to another member state. we have a lot of work to do. if reforms are to be linked to coordinated efforts to achieve european social security, this will make reforms significantly more difficult and it will be difficult to develop an effective solution. in this connection, it should be noted that enlargement is taking up a considerable part of the constrained financial resources. the report is therefore outside reality. pensions are becoming insecure, unsustainable and unpayable. no one wants to go backwards and the system that offers the most facilities should be adopted as a starting point. the european commission's document, on the other hand, provides a clear analysis of the problem. this document is characterised by a much more targeted approach. the report therefore offers no improvement over the commission document. this is why we have decided not to support this report, which can only undermine the sound approach proposed in the commission's communication.
in writing. -{nl) people live much longer than they are productive, at least if they have adequate health care, housing, food, working conditions and security. with work now threatening to become a form of high-level sport, people are prematurely exhausted and the need to retire at an earlier age is felt. in addition, families are now smaller, so that the proportion of younger generations is smaller than that of older generations; the number of people in employment per pensioner is therefore likely to decline in the future. over the past decades, most governments and businesses have come up with the wrong answer to this problem. the aim was to reduce the number of pensioners, notably by abolishing widow's allowances and raising the retirement age. they hoped to reduce contributions to the pension fund. in the meantime it has become clear that savings on pension rights can only lead to misery in the future. the only way to avoid this misery is a sharp and substantial increase in public spending. the real solution is to save in time to ensure a general right to a pension for everyone at the age of 60 and to improve disability pensions at a younger age. this report is not enough but it is moving in the right direction.

in writing. - (nl) compulsory military service, the use of soft drugs, the obligation to carry an identity document, abortion, euthanasia, the recognition of same-sex marriage - these are all matters which are regulated in very different ways by the member states. what is wrong with one is not wrong with the other. in this respect, the proposal does not entail any changes, and rightly so; even within a federation like the united states, penalties for criminal and misdemeanor offenses vary widely because decisions in this area are made at a subordinate level. however, this makes it difficult to enforce in one member state judgments given in another member state. should we lock people up for an act which is not wrong in the member state in question and then have the police violently suppress the outrage which this inevitably arouses? the proposal does not raise any problems if the offence which has been convicted is illegal in both member states and is punished by the same penalty. i regret that the report rejects this principle of 'double incrimination', although i understand that it reduces the opportunities for criminals to sabotage and delay proceedings by hiring expensive lawyers. i am, however, prepared to give this proposal the benefit of the doubt simply because recital ee provides for safeguard clauses because of differences between national laws.

the rapporteur. - mr president, i should like to open this debate by reading a poem: "is there one creature in the sky, on earth, in the water, that we are not the destroyer, that we don't spoil? no physical strength, no agility, and no ability to move. far less cunning or cunning can save them from our destructive power. no rock is so hard, no mountain so high and mighty, no tree so stately and full-grown: we can tear anything apart. no bird soars so high in the sky, no fish swims that deep in the sea, no animal lives that far away, in lonely places, or are we the ones who bring it into existence? we kill it. this poem expresses a deep compassion for creation. if you think it was written by a 21st century environmental activist, you are wrong, because it was published in 1536 by martin bucer, the vicar of st thomas' church in strasbourg. so caring for and taking care of the environment is certainly not a recent phenomenon. we are right to say that we are discussing today a commission communication and a parliament report which do not contain any startling news. the general opinion of the committee on the environment is that the european commission's communication bears too much resemblance to the document published six years ago. the policy developments in the intervening period are too weak for our liking. the commission's cautious approach is understandable in itself, but it must not lead to securing short-term economic growth as the highest political priority. other social and treaty objectives are then impeded. one of those other objectives is that economic development will be environmentally compatible. the commission should make it more clear to the member states that they have committed themselves to this and that they should follow through. the introduction of market-conform instruments allows the internalization of the external effects of economic activity in the prices of goods and services. this will help to assess more accurately the environmental scarcity that has so far been unaffordable. this gives producers and consumers 'automatic incentives' that steer them towards a more sustainable way of working and living. it is striking, however, that the commission does not pay attention to the imperfections and shadowy aspects of market functioning. clean air and clean drinking water should be freely available to everyone. this principle of social justice and equality should also be taken into account. the opinion of the economic and monetary committee is explicitly concerned with this. the problem of environmental degradation is not isolated. poverty, unemployment, energy and environmental problems interact and reinforce each other, threatening a negative spiral. not only in developing countries, but also in wealthy countries, this interaction occurs. this should be given more attention. as regards the indicators for the integration of the economy and the environment, the commission rightly calls for the structural indicators requested by the lisbon council to be included. unfortunately, the commission does not emphasize the great importance of a systematic approach linking environmental accounts to national accounts. parliament has already pointed this out in its 1995 and 1998 resolutions. the systematic approach is precisely the one which aims to provide an objective picture of the interaction between economic sectors, the environment and other fields. individual indicators create a much greater survey pressure. can commissioner wallström give an undertaking that this systematic approach will be followed in accordance with the proposals in the resolution before us? the commission's intention to tackle environmentally harmful subsidies and tax measures in the future has attracted considerable press attention. the suggestion to set up indicators for this, however, does not seem to me to be very fruitful. a critical review using a qualitative study that assesses the effectiveness of both environmentally harmful measures and environmental protection levies and incentive subsidies is much better. the communication does not address the consequences of the newly announced policy measures for the applicant countries. how are government or policy bodies from these countries involved in the process following this communication? public awareness of the importance of sustainable economic development is generally low. today's economic practice is one-sidedly geared towards greater expansion. it cannot be said that there is much respect for the preservation of creation and respect for the rights of others, including future generations. the present unequal global relations do not create rights for the inhabitants of rich, industrialized countries, but rather responsibilities and obligations. it is therefore regrettable that today's debate is announced under the heading 'environmental policy'. that's way too narrow. today we are talking about our future and whether we are prepared to participate in the process of change that was so promisingly launched in rio, or whether we are prepared to leave everything as it is. so the question is whether we take responsibility, whether we really want to be stewards of this earth.

draftsman of the opinion of the committee on budgetary control. – mr president, i will speak on behalf of the budgetary control committee and also on behalf of the socialist group. luckily the two positions are the same on this report. i would like to begin by thanking mr dell'alba for the excellent cooperation we have had on the financial regulation and all the colleagues that have worked with us in the different groups. most groups showed a great willingness to compromise. i would like to thank, in particular, the liberal, green, and edd groups for their active support in drawing up a package of amendments that was acceptable to a majority of the budgetary control committee. i was surprised, like my colleague mr dell'alba, that most amendments to this report were tabled by the chair of the budgetary control committee. i agree with mr dell'alba that, of course every member is entitled to put down amendments to a report, also on behalf of their group. in the case of a committee chair, however, you have to wonder whether they are mixing up roles to the detriment of the standing of their committee. these proposals today are the most sweeping changes to the community's financial rules in 21 years. for the budgetary control committee, the reform of financial control is the key aspect of this proposal. under the commission's proposal, the ex ante visa issued by a central financial controller will be abolished and instead directorates-general will be made fully responsible for the lifecycle of expenditure for programmes carried out under their authority. this is one of the key reforms called for by the committee of independent experts in 1999, when it issued its reports. the cie concluded, at the time, that most of the irregularities highlighted by the committee stemmed from decisions to which financial control gave its approval – the committee also stated that the supposed quality guarantee provided by the visa is a myth. it gave two strong arguments for changing the system and i quote, "first, ex ante checking, whether it be universal or on the basis of sampling is unlikely to be a cost-effective process. the efforts put into checking all transactions is clearly disproportionate while sampling is unlikely to have sufficient dissuasive effect. the second and fundamental principle is that any retention of ex ante control runs up against a crucial objection that de facto if not de jure, it displaces responsibility for financial irregularity from the person actually managing expenditure onto the person approving it. this displacement of responsibility means, in effect, that no one is ultimately responsible.” the court of auditors also discussed changes to the financial control regime in its opinion no 4 of 1997. with respect to the abolition of the ex ante visa it concluded as follows and i quote again, "as for completely abolishing the requirement of prior approval, this would not be any more acceptable unless it were to be replaced by other procedures that provided at least equivalent safeguards and that could involve financial officials other than the financial controller." has this test been met? broadly speaking, yes, at least according to court opinion no 2 of this year which commented on the commission's proposal as follows: the provisions governing the financial actors and therefore the structure of the community internal control system would represent an important step towards meeting the court's recommendations. the case for reform is overwhelming, that much is clear, but it is also to an extent a leap in the dark and it can only work if a number of conditions are met: first authorising officers must be held fully accountable; failure must be recognised and dealt with, not covered up. (the president urged the speaker to speak more slowly to assist the interpreters)the same interpreters refuse to translate into dutch when i speak english, but i am happy to oblige. second, the disciplinary procedure must be strengthened. there has been too little action in the past. a financial regularities committee would strengthen the procedure as would other amendments we have introduced. third, the independence of internal auditors must be guaranteed and so must the professional independence of those that carry out internal audit within the directorates-general. finally, minimum standards of financial controls must be adhered to. amendment no 72 sets this out. in order for this provision to be effective, there is a need for a central official under the responsibility of the dg budget to set minimum standards without undermining the responsibility of spending dgs. we will have to negotiate with the council on this proposal. the only possibility of doing so effectively is to postpone the vote on the legislative resolution under our rules of procedures. discussion on article 24 showed that the council does not pay the slightest attention to parliament's views, even though the president of the budgets committee is here today, and that is particularly surprising coming from the swedish presidency. i have been approached in recent weeks by a number of national governments asking us to proceed with our vote without delay. the sad fact in today's institutional set-up is that if parliament wants its voice to be heard it must resort to unusual tactics. i support the case for speedy reform, but on an issue as important as this – financial rules which could with us for the next 21 years – we must refuse to let parliament's legitimate expectations to negotiate be ignored by an arrogant council.

in writing. - (nl) in the past, most companies were small and their activities were linked to a city or region. their assets were not anonymous and the staff remained attached to the company throughout their lives. for a long time, public authorities have supported efforts to keep firms in the hands of regional or national ownership, or to create firms on a non-commercial basis, which are better able to serve the interests of workers and consumers. in a society where all interests are subordinated to market liberalism and global competition, companies have now become consumer goods. when this is acceptable to buyers and former shareholders, companies close down because their profit margins are lower than those of the rest of the group, their brand name can be applied to other products or their production site can be transferred to a country where wages are lower and environmental legislation is less restrictive. the consequences for employment, for social cohesion around the business, for consumers and for the scope for democratically defined government policy are extremely negative. this is why transparent, controllable and small companies are still far preferable to giant companies that operate on a global scale and constantly surprise and dictate to others. mergers in which trade unions and the public authorities are not given a right of veto lead to clashes and misfortune. i am against these commercial practices and i am voting against the proposal.
in writing. - (nl) due to the functioning of the market, where the aim is to find the best electricity market and not the most environmentally friendly, the threat of the resurgence of polluting fuels such as nuclear energy, coal, lignite and oil is looming. in the netherlands, relatively clean power stations are left idle to make way for cheap but polluting energy imports. replacing these polluting fuels with solar, wind and hydroelectric energy is essential to preserving our environment. instead of actively working on developing new forms of electricity generation, consumers are first asked to buy more environmentally friendly energy at a different price from another supplier. today, the amount of clean electricity these suppliers are able to supply is less than the demand of the consumer. this situation has led to attempts to attribute several forms of electricity production to renewable energy. the incineration of unsorted organic household waste and wood waste has always existed and suddenly this practice is being put in the category of renewable energy in order to achieve the set target. my support for renewable energy production does not fall into the latter category. significant investment in new sources of renewable energy that anticipate consumer demand and are not dependent on waste collection is an alternative to the system now required by the council.
in writing. - (nl) entrepreneurs have discovered occupational pension funds as a source of venture capital. the leaders consider these institutions to be part of an integrated financial market which should contribute to the competitiveness of the european economy. in the hope that the returns of pension funds will increase, managers entrust them to companies whose sole objective is to generate profits. in the near future, shareholders of banks and insurance companies will reap these benefits, pensioners will bear the increased risk of the disappearance of protection mechanisms, and the disadvantages of changing employers or member states will not be addressed. the proposal for a european directive does not take into account the reasons which led to the creation of these pension reserves. pensions are a means of distributing and supplementing people's incomes in order to ensure a sustainable and acceptable standard of living for all, even when, at the age of 70, 90 or 110, these people will no longer be productive. a public pension scheme providing a reasonable and equal pension for all is the best guarantee that no one will be deprived of his right to income. the occupational pensions are only advantageous for people with a fixed, high-paying job. these schemes offer no solution to people who have been forced to change their employer or job frequently. this is especially true for private supplementary pensions, which are only available to those who are able and willing to invest individual funds with an insurance company during productive years.

in writing. - (nl) on the eve of the compulsory exchange of the coins and notes of eleven member states for euros, our attention is focused on the exasperation that will result shortly after the changeover to 2002. mr maaten's proposals seek to speed up and facilitate this process somewhat. however, the fundamental problem is more related to the european central bank's annual report 2000. unlike the rapporteur, mrs randzio-plath, i do not see why the ecb should be praised. the value of the euro was to be maintained by means of a stability pact which obliged national governments to reduce the level of their expenditure and to abandon the borrowing of money. this policy proved to be a complete failure, given that the parity of the euro against the dollar was not maintained, not temporarily but over a longer period. meanwhile, in several member states, including the netherlands, annual inflation is already above the interest rate. price stability is unlikely to be maintained in the new year. the acquisition by the euro of the status of an international means of payment similar to the dollar seems to us to be compromised. this is why we are also unable, like the americans, to pass on part of the public deficit to the rest of the world, which continues to struggle at the gates of a currency whose exchange rate is falling. in other words, the failure of the ecb's performance forces us to reject this annual report.

- mr president, anyone who thinks that apartheid has been abolished is wrong. this still exists as a caste system in india and neighboring countries. the european human rights policy has hitherto been wrongfully silent on this flagrant injustice. in india, systematic discrimination has deep historical roots and is fully integrated into the social system. one hundred and sixty million people from the lowest caste are trapped in the dungeons of cultural and religious tradition. there is legislation against the system, but the practice of society does not care. a dalit or untouchable is a person without a chance from birth and is condemned to a life of humiliation and an existence on the margins of society. dalits are routinely abused by the upper caste. women are raped and no one gets justice. there is a systematic inequality of opportunity. social mobility, one of the hallmarks of a genuine democracy, is completely out of the question. india is not only the largest democracy in the world, but also the most undemocratic. there is no cultural or religious justification for the structural violation of universal human rights. in india itself, awareness of the inhumanity of society is slowly breaking through, but there is a great reluctance to change among those who benefit from it. the caste system is a culturally entrenched form of political and economic exploitation. a massive campaign of awareness must be launched and europe must put this gross form of racial discrimination on the international agenda, starting with the forthcoming world conference on racism in durban. it is not an easy task, but we must be courageous, said mr michel before he disappeared. we shouldn't pretend the entire caste system itself is untouchable. apartheid is only unchangeable if we accept it, and we should not. i would like to hear the commission and the council's reaction.

commission. – president-in-office, ladies and gentlemen, i would like on behalf of the commission to thank mrs jackson for raising such an important issue in the house. as the president-in-office has already said, in gothenburg, the heads of state and government confirmed that the european community and the member states are determined to meet their commitments under the kyoto protocol. the union’s summit reaffirmed the european union’s aim of bringing the protocol into force by 2002 and asked the commission to prepare a proposal for ratification before the end of 2001. regrettably, the bush administration continues to oppose the kyoto protocol. at the european union/united states summit in gothenburg, president bush acknowledged the science underlying climate change and the global importance of this issue. the united states has indicated that while they will participate actively in the resumed cop6 in bonn, their basic position, opposing the protocol has not changed. we will build upon this indication that the united states does not intend to obstruct the kyoto process. to facilitate this, we have agreed that there will be further high-level contacts with the united states on this subject. the resumed cop6 in july will pick up the threads of the conference in the hague and try and bring the negotiations to a successful conclusion. to achieve this, the european union will take a positive attitude while, at the same time, being realistic about what can be achieved. the new consolidated texts by the chairman of cop6, mr pronk, are clear and concise and provide a good basis for the bonn negotiations. however, the texts still contain a number of important sticking points for the european union, notably on funding for developing countries, compliance and supplementarity. these need to be resolved. in the end, we will strive for an overall package where compromises on one side are balanced out by gains on the other. we must also take into account the specific importance of japan and russia for the entry into force of the protocol. the commission welcomes the strong interest of the european parliament in the global problem of climate change and the participation of members of the european parliament in the community delegation to the resumed cop6. as in the hague, the commission and council, the president-in-office has explained, have proposed that the european parliament be represented by eight members. in accordance with the institutional rules for their participation, the members can attend plenary meetings, and the commission will regularly provide information on those negotiations which are not open to observers on a regular basis to all members of the european parliament present at cop6.

- mr president, the structure of the fishing fleet is determined by the socioeconomic conditions of a region, by the total allowed catch (tac) and the quotas combined with technical measures. the measures to ensure that the fishing fleet is not over-exploited. the commission has already made considerable progress in this respect, in 1999 taking into account for the first time the countries unit of effort. on the other hand, greater engine power does not necessarily mean greater fishing effort, considering that the freezing capacity on some vessels also requires additional engine power. in writing. - (nl) human society cannot exist without enterprises producing goods and providing services. this fact should not make us forget that some companies can also be a threat to society. they want as few taxes as possible, as little worker participation as possible and as few rules as possible to protect against environmental pollution and animal abuse. large companies in particular seek to achieve the greatest possible profit for the owners and often also seek the best possible options for management. this lure of profit is often thwarted by efforts to ensure the healthiest possible environment, the prevention of occupational diseases, a safe working environment, democratic decision-making and the desire to have sufficient financial resources to cover the costs of collective equipment. it is therefore necessary to organise the widest possible publicity, so that the whole of society can also judge what companies are doing. in addition, companies which infringe these rules must not, under any circumstances, receive any contribution from european funds.
in writing. - (nl) no company can function without the people who do the work. the workers have a good knowledge of what is wrong and how to improve the situation. this knowledge is often denied, because these people have not been engaged to make judgments. traditional power relations are based on the principle that only ownership and management matter. the workforce seems to be nothing more than a necessary evil, which has nothing to do with the company but is merely temporarily engaged in the outside world. in the event of reorganisation, the shareholders and the bosses decide, with the workforce being the ancillary position. thousands of people may leave because another product requiring other skills is considered more profitable, because production is offshored to a country where wages are lower or even because workers are punished for their wishes to improve. unfortunately, the rapporteur does not propose that workers should be given a right of free access to information and a suspensive veto. a suspensive veto allows, on the one hand, to seek and develop first alternatives, in full transparency and using all available expertise and, on the other hand, to end the monopoly of the management and owners of the company in the event of restructuring.

- mr president, more than a year ago the temporary committee on echelon and other large-scale interception systems began its work. there were serious doubts at the time as to whether this committee message traffic. it also states that other countries, including most of the member states of the european union, also use systems to intercept international telecommunications. at the same time, however, the report dispels the myth that every telephone call is monitored and every fax or e-mail is read via echelon and similar systems. it is not technically possible, and most countries are democracies with clear limits on the activities of the secret services, at least in relation to their own citizens. we know, in particular, from information published by the dutch and german governments in the course of the echelon commission's investigation, that systems for intercepting international telecommunications are used primarily as a tool in the fight against international terrorism, human trafficking, drug trafficking, the illegal arms trade and in the enforcement of internationally established embargoes. and nobody is against that, at least if it is done with proper secret services and the lack of openness of many governments prevent the use of systems for interception of international telecommunications in a more transparent manner. clear and enforceable rules european union. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the euro against counterfeiting. effective democratic and political control of the activities of secret services, and thus also of the interception of international telephone communications, is an indispensable component of the right of any state to defend itself against external attacks on the security of its citizens or on its democratic structure. we need a cultural shift. it is inevitable that some aspects of the work of the intelligence service must remain secret, but there is also a great deal that can indeed bear the light of openness and democracy. only countries which deal with their intelligence services in an open and fair manner vis-à-vis their citizens will also be able to achieve the necessary cooperation at european level and will be able to contribute to the creation of a european intelligence capacity in the context of an effective common foreign and security policy. the traditional distrust of outsiders by the intelligence services and the traditional preference for national interests must be transformed into cooperation, which completely overshadows the uk-us treaty on which echelon is based. not only because it was agreed at the european summit in helsinki that a european intelligence capacity would be in writing. -(nl) in the netherlands, many people put stickers on their mailboxes stating that they do not want to receive commercial printed material. slowly, it became commonly accepted that it was incorrect and even unjustified to ignore this type of request. over time, this type of scheme has been called an opt-out scheme, because it is up to the recipient to say yes or no to receiving commercial mail. an opt-in scheme, whereby people would have to specify that they wish to receive commercial mail, would be even better. it would be even more appropriate in the field of electronic communication. the consumer would then be protected against receiving and sending untimely advertisements, which he would also have to pay for. in addition, the result of this flood of advertisements is that our e-mail inboxes are overloaded, making it impossible to use them to communicate reliably. the commission is therefore right to propose the introduction of an opt-in system in article 13. i am concerned about the rapporteur's view, since he seems to prefer an opt-out system, which only relieves the consumer of the inconvenience after he has expressly protested. it should also be noted that negative experiences have already taken place as a result of promises made by organisations that make money from direct marketing. the protection of privacy rightly pursued by the directive is seriously jeopardized by mr cappato's views.

expectations of those who advocate the liberalisation of the energy market, in other words if we did not make demands or allow exceptions to generate electricity from old, polluting plants, then in our view the market mechanism would be disrupted and those who neglect the environment would be rewarded with a head start because they would be able to use their old plants to lower energy prices. since the council did not wish to accept parliament's amendments, conciliation was necessary, which was combined with the riitta myller report. i thank her, too. she was an excellent partner in those negotiations. the trialogue with the swedish presidency and the commission in may and june this year also saw considerable progress made on reducing emissions of so2, sulphur dioxide, and on a number fuels and domestic brown coal. unfortunately, we did not really reach agreement at the first meeting on the most important point for me, nox. after the first reading we had taken a big step forward when the council agreed to include old installations in the directive. this was important because those old plants are often the least energy efficient and also emit disproportionately high greenhouse gases. the compromise reached in the conciliation procedure allowed the european parliament to tighten up the proposed limit values for so2 and nox. the council agreed, almost immediately, to a substantial reduction in so2, particularly for medium and large combustion plants, which are also the most efficient. as regards nox emissions, parliament has insisted on reducing the nox limit value for large combustion plants from 650 mg per cubic metre to 200 mg for those plants burning solid fuels. however, these limits will only apply to new and existing installations from 2016. that's too late. as i said, some member states have already introduced these standards a year or three ago. we did not say no to it because it was an important step forward and also because it is an important condition which will be imposed on the applicant countries in the future. we have also been able to bring down the exception which the council wanted for peak installations, so that polluting considered possible at the second reading. i thank the swedish presidency. i thank all my colleagues, particularly mrs myller. i thank the commission for its constructive support. i therefore recommend, on behalf of the delegation, that this proposal be adopted.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, our citizens are increasingly affected by noise. ten years ago, the european commission estimated that a quarter of our citizens suffer from noise. today, the european environment agency estimates that 30% of europeans suffer from noise. a 20 percent increase in ten years. in my country, the netherlands, noise affects as much as 43%. more than ten million citizens in europe suffer from sleep disorders. all citizens in europe have the right to the same protection against noise-induced illness. unfortunately, our environment ministers have a different view. unfortunately, the council did not follow the proposal of the vast majority of the european parliament at its first reading to come up with four subsidiary directives. subsidiary directives for motorways, air traffic, railways and factories. the commission therefore proposes four subsidiary directives. the european parliament is about a combined approach! the european union is committed to reducing the noise of european aircraft and to the same noise standards around busy airports to protect our citizens. the commission has also proposed a directive on the protection of the environment against the emission of gaseous and particulate pollutants from motor vehicles. the commission has also proposed a directive on noise reduction in european trains and the same noise standards on busy railways. the commission has already proposed a number of measures to reduce noise in factories and to limit its penetration of the outside world. the council followed the view of the dutch minister for the environment, jan pronk, that noise is only a local problem. our environment ministers are exposing our citizens to more and more noise. on the subject of road, air and rail noise, the environment ministers have only proposed a weak declaration, but no binding legislation. there are now only a few european noise standards, such as for household appliances, lawn mowers and high-speed lines. european noise standards for aircraft are urgently needed. the world organization icao proposes only modest noise reduction for new aircraft. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. european standards for lorries and cars are either not in place or are far too weak. the tyre directive is a good example of this. silent tyres are available on the european market but are not yet mandatory. with whispering asphalt, a tremendous noise reduction of ten to thirteen decibels can be achieved. these technical possibilities must be incorporated into european policy. in addition to european standards for high-speed trains, standards are also needed for conventional passenger trains and for freight trains. the council did agree to harmonize the measurement and calculation of noise. there are now 51 different methods of doing this in europe. the same directive reduces them to two: lden and lnight. unfortunately, the council has dropped a few stitches here. the environment committee proposes to correct it. the majority of the committee on the environment has also dropped a few minor points. the green group therefore tabled four additional amendments together with the socialist group. slightly lower noise levels should also be measured. the european commission shares this view and i invite the commissioner to confirm this publicly. the common position states that the aim of the action plans is to mitigate noise. in plain dutch, that means soundproofing and double glazing. but that's not enough. the action plans should also be aimed at reducing noise. the majority of the committee on the environment has followed the council in its view that a member state should be able to set the noise indicator lden differently. this means that there is no longer any harmonised measurement but that the additional protection of the night can be reduced by a factor of ten, from eight hours to six hours. that is capitulation to the lobbies and has nothing to do with the cultural differences between our peoples. that eight-hour sleep period is essential for everyone. that is why we have tabled a joint amendment here. i call on all my colleagues to think this over carefully and not to be drawn into the lobbying on wednesday but to give priority to protecting the health of our citizens.

- mr president, the country of origin principle must provide an answer to the challenge of offering financial services electronically. one word of caution. first of all, the scope for national policy. the country of origin principle respects national law. in addition, member states may derogate from the principle of country of origin. that's only allowed for very specific reasons. the rapporteur could therefore have given more detailed reasons for the effect of the principle on national policy in the report. that might have prevented some unfortunate socialist amendments. the report also bases itself on the assumption that more competition will only benefit consumers. he needs to know what rules the provider is following. otherwise, the confidence in e-commerce will not increase. the rapporteur should therefore have dealt more specifically with consumer protection at european level. if bottlenecks arise, it may be difficult to make exceptions, as not all member states will agree with the need for them. it is therefore important to continue to monitor whether the practice will be satisfactory for providers and consumers.

in writing. -(nl) it is an old practice to isolate political opponents by calling them terrorists. when former terrorists became the leaders of south africa, israel, the palestinian authority and a very large number of former colonies, they suddenly became reasonable and respectable in the eyes of many people, and their opponents then were rightly blamed for causing the violence. by excluding any possibility of nonviolent improvement, they had driven the opposition to despair. that is why we must always distinguish between opposition, namely action for socio-economic and administrative change, and blind violence focused exclusively on anguish and destruction. the us list of 27 suspected islamist-based organisations raises the suspicion in a number of cases that support for governments in the fight against international terrorism has been bought by also labelling their domestic opposition as terrorists. in this case we are making the same mistake as in the case of the criminalization of abortion, euthanasia and the sale of soft drugs by the inhabitants of member states, whereas this is permitted by the judicial authorities of other member states. in the just fight against real terrorism, not everything that is proposed now is fair or targeted. i do not support this reckless approach.

in writing. -{nl) wave movements, with their ups and downs, are part of the characteristics of a market economy. at a time when economic growth is stagnating or consumption is declining, it is foolish to push people to be unjustifiably optimistic. such optimism is then a form of deception and leads to reckless consumption and risky investments. it would be preferable to extend public measures or to relaunch new ones. it was the method that brought roosevelt's america out of the crisis in the 1930s and the successful reconstruction of western europe after 1945. it is also the method by which authoritarian states such as nazi germany and the soviet union have managed to build economies that are much stronger than the outside world had imagined. in all these cases, whether they are considered sympathetic or not, the system has satisfied many people in unexpected ways. instead of learning from them, we now return to the primitive views of the 19th and early 20th centuries that preceded these successes. tax cuts, in favour of high incomes and large companies, are now seen as positive and public works as very negative. the report by mrs peijs is in line with this trend. the results i see are poverty and instability, so i cannot agree.

- mr president, once again there are problems with a patent granted by the european patent office. whereas in march 2000 a patent was sought for the manipulation of human cells and embryos, this time we are faced with a patent on human breast cancer genes. let me be clear: - and i repeat what i have said before, including in contributions on directive 98/44/ec on the legal protection of biotechnological inventions - a patent can and should only be obtained or granted for an invention and not for a discovery! i urge the european patent office to do the same. otherwise, before long the entire human genome will be patented! and what will be the next step: a modified cell, an organism? i'm holding my heart. but back to the patent on a breast cancer gene. what's the problem, anyway? how can the european patent office grant a patent on a human gene? the answer is simple: because they apply directive 98/44/ec. despite the fact that only a few member states have implemented the directive in question and despite the resolutions of the european parliament. why is directive 98/44/ec so controversial? let me explain it to you again: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. let's not make this any more complicated than it is: article 5 (1) and (2) are in contradiction. article 5 (1) of the directive reads as follows: 'the human body at the various stages of its formation and development, and the mere discovery of any of its parts, including a sequence or partial sequence of a gene, are not patentable.' article 5 (2) of the treaty states: 'a part of the human body which has been isolated or otherwise obtained by a technical process, including a sequence or partial sequence of a gene, is patentable even if the structure of that part is identical to that of a natural part.' in other words: 5.1 says: no patent on a gene, whereas 5.2 says, the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment. but every gene that researchers work with is engineered! let us therefore do everything we can to remove this inconsistency from directive 98/44/ec. i am not against these steps by the european patent office just because a patent on a gene is against the concept of patenting. another important consideration is that i see life in all its facets and components as god's creation. this also leads me to believe that a gene is not patentable. i said in march 2000 that directive 98/44/ec would continue to be a subject of debate. after heated debates in the temporary committee on human genetics and after today, i can say that that estimate was correct.
- i am surprised that the commission has not responded. one of them. secondly, i would ask the commission whether it is indeed prepared to do something before 10 october. when i talk about a gene, i'm also talking about a sequence of a gene. and a gene sequence is not patentable under the patent directive.

in writing. -the second wave of the feminist movement in the 1960s and 1970s aimed to give women access to paid employment. women had, on average, less education than men, and even when they had higher education, men, who were omnipotent, often relegated them to menial jobs with lower status and pay. in addition, many wives were financially dependent on their husbands. women with higher education were rightly demanding jobs which, at that time, were almost automatically denied them. the fate of less educated women was usually different. cleaning offices or rearranging supermarket shelves was not an insurmountable task, and in many cases it was no more rewarding than the role of housewife. these women felt liberated when their husbands earned a salary that allowed them to stay at home. in time, most women found paid employment without the men working less or staying at home to take care of and raise the children. unintentionally, feminism became a tool to fill the shortage of staff that employers complained about while limiting public spending. in such circumstances, it is all the more essential to actively combat all forms of discrimination and bullying in the workplace.
in writing. -(nl) most of the companies that used to consume the energy produced at chernobyl, and which made it possible to finance the maintenance of such a gigantic nuclear reactor complex, have disappeared since the collapse of the soviet union. the ukrainian population is in such a state of poverty that only a minority of people have sufficient purchasing power to afford abundant electricity consumption. there is also not enough money in the country to finance new, greener and safer methods of electricity generation, and given the long half-life of radioactive materials, there will be a lot of water still flowing under bridges before it is possible to talk about liquidating the remains of the destroyed power plants. no operation there is conceivable without outside help. the measures to provide chernobyl with a new protection massif by 2005 are too modest and too late. behind the first building erected just after the 1986 disaster, a dangerous fire continues to burn, so that nuclear energy remains a source of risk for the future. in the debate on 2 may, 15 years after chernobyl, i had already pointed out that other types of nuclear power stations were not safe and that their dismantling would not solve all the problems. despite all these shortcomings, i will support this funding proposal, because to refrain from acting would certainly not solve anything.
- president. - first of all, i would like to thank mr poos for his report on the necessary reforms in the council. it is said of the pope that you don't have to be married to talk about marriage. mr poos is entitled to speak about the council because he has been a member of it for a very long time. the council's poor functioning at crucial moments was demonstrated at the ghent summit, where three prime ministers made advance arrangements outside the council, where the president of the council made essential statements on the evaluation of the attacks on afghanistan which were later not covered by the council, where several prime ministers made different statements at the european summit, where decisions were taken on a question of bank payments in relation to the euro but no decisions were taken on crucial anti-terrorism measures proposed by the commission and parliament and where finally there was also a difficult dispute between the president of the council and the president of the commission. that is the public image of the council, and that bad image dominates all decision-making and all image-making in the union. how can the council be reformed in such a way that the union functions better and that the image of the citizens is also improved? how can the council be reformed in such a way that the whole institutional structure of the union becomes more democratic and open? i think there are a few factors that are crucial. firstly, the council must confine itself to its original purpose, namely to express the views of the governments of the member states, subject to the control of the national parliaments and the european parliament. secondly, the council must coordinate its work better so that the general affairs council and the specialized councils speak with one voice. i think that the number of committees could be reduced even further. thirdly, the general affairs council should function much more strongly, and on the basis of strong positions of national officials for european affairs, preferably in the capacity of minister. belgium has set a good example in this respect. fourthly, when it comes to legislation, including the budget, all council meetings must be public, which means that both deliberations and decision-making are public and publicly reported. fifthly, in legislation, including the budget, only ministers should be given voting rights, which means that they cannot be replaced by, for example, the permanent representative or by officials. i believe that the council should function in full accordance with its real role as a federal council on the german model, so that the role of the council in the democratic process of the union is made clear to the citizens. i very much hope that mr poos' report will play an important role at the forthcoming igc and i hope above all that the council will take to heart what is being criticised here in parliament, but also praised here and there.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of ships is not compromised. we discussed this subject at first reading on 12 february last. the commission proposal for a directive was related to the high number of accidents involving bulk carriers. research has shown that many of these accidents were due to the condition of the ship's wall. damage to the wall, combined with the wave action, could be fatal. inventory of procedures and practice showed that bulk carriers were regularly damaged during loading or unloading. it also showed that procedures to prevent damage to bulk carriers are hardly being applied. an international code has been drawn up which sets out the basic safety principles for loading and unloading: the bulk loading and unloading code, the blu code. these principles describe procedures to be followed before, during and after loading and unloading bulk carriers. two of the main points are: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the port authorities are able to carry out the necessary checks and inspections. despite imo calls for the blu code to be transposed into national legislation, this has not yet been done in many countries. the european commission wants to improve this. the commission is proposing to amend the directive to include a new category of goods, namely motor vehicles, and to introduce a new category of goods. the commission proposal therefore aims to incorporate the blu code into community legislation. it also requires terminals to establish a quality assurance system to ensure that the quality of loading and unloading operations is at a constantly satisfactory level. it is also intended to be the land-based counterpart of the ism safety system for bulk carriers on the seaward side. parliament approved the basic idea of this proposal at its first reading on 13 february 2001 and supported 14 amendments to it. the main amendments concerned two subjects: firstly, the obligation of the competent authorities to intervene in the loading and unloading process as soon as they become aware of a dangerous situation for the crew or the ship. secondly, to improve the flow of information between the actors concerned. the council has accepted most of these amendments in its common position, namely at least 11 of them. three amendments were therefore not adopted. the council also added a number of elements to the proposal. i should like to comment briefly on these elements and on the three amendments which were not adopted. firstly, the scope is somewhat limited. the directive now applies to ships which call at ports in the european union and are not unloaded with their own equipment. furthermore, terminal operators may limit their inspection and information activities to those areas for which they are directly responsible. secondly, the council has made some changes to the compulsory quality assurance system. a landing delay has been added for new terminals, while existing terminals have been given three years to comply with the requirements. another new aspect is that equivalent systems are allowed in addition to iso 9001:2000. thus, terminals which already have an appropriate quality system do not have to install another equivalent system at high cost. thirdly, the council has added to the amendments which improve reporting and reporting between the various actors. the three points which the council ultimately did not accept concern minor amendments to recital 13, article 10 (1) and (2). in addition, some amendments were made to the annexes, removing some unnecessary provisions and introducing some safety guarantees. mr president, after evaluating all the amendments by the council, my conclusion is that the council has accepted the essential amendments of parliament. the remaining amendments are not of such importance that a longer delay in the introduction and application of this legislation is justified. the recommendation that i and the committee on transport in this parliament make is therefore to adopt the common position unchanged and to urge its rapid implementation and application in the member states.

- mr president, commissioner, if policy instruments are not working well, they are adapted and if they are not working, they are abolished. it is with this principle in mind that i was unpleasantly surprised by the present commission proposal. i understand that the commission does not want to introduce a new structural policy which could be rendered obsolete within a year by the reform of the fisheries policy. but i am not immune to the impression that the commission still does not realise that it is fishing behind the net with the current multiannual guidance programmes. the desire to manage fisheries with two different instruments - tacs and quotas on the one hand and fleet structure policy on the other - leads to serious problems, especially since these policy instruments serve different purposes. tacs and quotas are the key factors in fisheries management. however, sustainable fishing can only be achieved if there is room within the allowable catch limits for an efficient fleet. fleet structure policy should be supportive in this respect. unfortunately, that is not the case. thanks to the mop, all kinds of subsidies have been used to maintain the fleet's overcapacity and thus distortion of competition. in addition, a number of member states have introduced incentive measures which further distort competition. the common fisheries policy has a clear objective, and the system of tacs and quotas should be the determining factor. this is a necessary condition for a well-functioning control system with strict penalties. for the time being, however, the commission is sticking to its mop, with some changes which i cannot but call unfortunate. in one of these amendments, the commission, under the guise of strengthening the effectiveness of the mop, ignores the most elementary sense of the law. by withholding public aid, it penalizes one fisheries segment for the overcapacity in another. the commission's discrimination in respect of fleet capacity reductions further undermines fairness. the fleet in my country regulates capacity by reducing activity (the sea days system). unlike other countries, the netherlands is now excluded from european aid for new construction. in order to undo these unfortunate changes, we will wholeheartedly support the rapporteur's amendments.

the rapporteur. − mr president, this week the european parliament will be holding the preliminary round of the debate on the 'public administration' regulation. in technical terms, the regulation is called 'access to documents', but in popular parlance it has been given a different name. in may, after months of negotiations with the council and the commission, we were able to conclude the regulation with a positive content. for me personally, it was an important moment, because i have been working for years for more transparency in the european union. the regulation requires each of the institutions, the commission, the council and parliament, to ensure that the regulation is incorporated into their own rules of procedure, in their rules of procedure and in their rules of procedure before 3 december. for our parliament, this meant that we had to go through our rules of procedure to see if there were any improvements to be made. we often feel that the commission and the council are the ones who are lacking in this area, but we have found that there is still room for some amendments in our rules of procedure. i would like to say, mr president, that when i speak of 'we', i want to emphasize that i also want to include my colleague, mr cashman, with whom i have worked closely. the assessment was made in the committee on constitutional affairs, but also in the committee on civil liberties and human rights. this is logical, since the two committees have also worked together at an earlier stage. i would like to thank mr cashman very much for the constructive way in which we have always been able to hold our discussions. what are the proposed changes to our rules of procedure for which we ask your support? firstly, it concerns the right of all citizens of the european union, including citizens of third countries, to have access to european parliament documents. this right was granted to european citizens, but not to third-country nationals registered in the eu. so there is a need for an enlargement that did not yet exist. this is in line with the us freedom of information act. so we're not doing anything special here. secondly, the definition of
