the rapporteur. - president, i also welcome commissioner byrne, who can do a lot in this area. there is much to be said about the implementation of directive 95/29/ec and the transport of animals. the lack of adequate controls, the lack of due diligence on the part of transporters and abuses in the export of slaughter animals outside the eu are causing a great deal of commotion. in addition, the unrestricted movement of slaughter animals through the european union has aggressively contributed to the spread of livestock diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease and swine fever. it is striking that the consequences of this are borne almost entirely by livestock farmers. the abuses committed during transport and the spread of livestock diseases have direct consequences for the image and often the income of livestock farmers, while they have no part in the causes mentioned. so those who want to prevent livestock diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease and swine fever, those who are concerned about the already difficult situation of european livestock farmers and those who have a heart for animal welfare will not tolerate a culture of tolerance and confused rules for the transport of animals. the fact that parliament has decided to present an own-initiative proposal for the tightening up of the above directives at this stage is a strong political signal to the council and the commission. the council will be holding a conference next month on european vaccination policy and this report makes a first proposal for effective prevention of infectious animal diseases. the commission will also shortly be putting forward proposals to further tighten up the rules on the transport of animals. the report also shows parliament's deep dissatisfaction with the implementation of existing legislation by the member states and the commission's limited ability to impose fines on member states. the report is intended, mr president, to set out the main lines of good legislation on the transport of animals. first of all, the control. the control of animal transport in the european union must be brought to a european level by the following measures. firstly, the appointment of 15 eu inspectors who will be required to report annually to the council, the commission, but also to the european parliament and the parliaments of the member states. the second point is the appropriate rules for sanctions, both financial and in terms of authorizations. the third point concerns the introduction of an adequate european licensing system for animal transporters. i would like to make the following points concerning the transport time. for animals for slaughter and for consumption, we propose a limitation of the transport time to four hours or 250 km, with an extension to eight hours possible, provided the transporter has a licence and the animals can lie down and have fresh water. for breeding and sporting animals we suggest a transport time of twice 24 hours by specialised transporters, provided the animals have fresh water and feed. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. for areas with few or no slaughterhouses, the commission may grant a derogation up to a maximum of 50% of the increase in the distance and time mentioned. for small islands, but also for ireland - and i would like to emphasize ireland in particular - there is a separate system for transport by ship. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's food safety legislation is applied in the regions concerned, and i therefore propose that the structural funds be allocated to these regions for investments in small and semi-mobile slaughterhouses. the export refund for the export of live slaughter should be terminated as soon as possible. but this cannot be done without initiating an international debate on the transport of slaughtered animals and putting this subject on the agenda. the amendments are as follows. i have tabled three amendments with the liberal and socialist group to make the report more practical. it concerns amendments nos 4, 5 and 6, amongst others on temperature, but also a number of other practical points. i also thank my colleagues heinz kindermann and neil busk for their very constructive cooperation. i think that the report should also be called the maat-busk-kindermann report. i assume that the liberal group will withdraw amendment no 3, since it is identical to the joint amendment of the ppe-de, pse and eldr. the policy of tolerance and the free-for-all surrounding the transport of animals must be stopped. literally millions of animals have been killed and destroyed in the eu over the last four years as a result of an explosion of animal diseases, for example foot-and-mouth disease and swine fever. the abuses in the transport of animals and the shocking images of them are an indictment of european culture, of which care for animals and the countryside is an essential part. the sad thing is that in all cases the farmer is paying the real price at a time when meat prices are unacceptably low and consumer prices are unprecedentedly high. commission and council, it is time for action, time to choose the quality of our livestock and our countryside.

- mr president, the arrival of the euro is creating great expectations among the citizens. one of these expectations is that the use of the euro will result in the same price being paid for the use of means of payment in the member states concerned. it is therefore not good that shortly before the introduction of the euro the question of the fees for crossborder payments has not been adequately resolved. the banks and financial institutions are to blame for this. self-regulation in the sector is clearly not working. i therefore greatly appreciate the efforts of commissioner bolkestein and rapporteur peijs, who have worked hard to find a solution. there are good reasons for banks to not charge any fees for electronic crossborder payments. the current technology allows these payment transactions to be carried out at low cost and the same technology is also possible for cross-border payments. the use of different rates is undesirable and contrary to the idea of the internal payments market and a common currency. for banks, electronic payment means savings by encouraging less labour-intensive pin payments. i therefore support the line of the european commission and the rapporteur, mr peijs, and express the hope that the rapid introduction of this measure will strengthen consumer confidence in the euro.

mr president, i note that the katiforis report does not explain why the european commission's proposal to amend the excise duty rates on tobacco is rejected. apparently, this position cannot be substantiated. the new proposal is an amendment to existing directives, so the legal basis is not in question. the reason for the change is that member states miss a large number of excise duties through fraud and smuggling. the internal market is not yet fully operational and competition is being distorted. if the differences between member states are reduced, these fraud and smuggling will be discouraged and hopefully even disappear. moreover, the necessary increase in tobacco excise duties for a number of member states as a result of this proposal will not harm health. for the reasons i have mentioned, i can support a minimum pressure of 57%. the european commission should take additional measures if the smuggling practices, which even tobacco manufacturers are involved in, do not disappear. i have repeatedly called for the cessation of subsidies to tobacco. i can therefore wholeheartedly support mr maaten's amendments. the european union is still very unreliable on this point. on the one hand, tobacco use is discouraged by warning messages, bans on tobacco advertising and higher excise duties, while on the other hand, a billion euros is lost in the form of tobacco subsidies. the support for tobacco growers to switch to other crops, which is also subsidized, is a very generous solution and therefore deserves the support of parliament. i therefore call on the council to support the proposals of the european commission and not to give in to the pressure of one or two member states. i object, moreover, to mr folias's appropriation of common sense. i have as much right to say that everyone has the right to his own stupidity.

in writing. -(nl) the european union is made up of sovereign states, each of which has a seat at the united nations and, until now, its own currency. banks are part of the international payment circuits and charge large amounts for domestic transfers and withdrawals. from january 2002, 12 eu member states will become one country in financial terms. banks are in favour of this development as long as it broadens their playing field but not if they have to give up additional transfers from their customers. it would be interesting to require the same conditions for domestic and crossborder payments in euro. this is the wish that has been expressed for some time by commissioner bolkestein and which is now also expressed in mrs peijs' report. i am prepared to support it as long as the banks do not charge any more for crossborder transfers. however, recital 5a does not preclude them from using new levies on domestic payments to compensate for the disappearance of income from cross-border transfers. rather than imposing large charges on a small minority of transfers, mostly commercial transfers, all payments would be affected. in other words, the vast majority of customers would face higher costs. since this would be a serious disadvantage to the ordinary account holder, i shall vote against this proposal.
in writing. -{nl) the human being is itself largely composed of water and water constitutes a significant part of our diet. at work and at home, water is a part of many of our daily activities. we could not live without a constant supply of water. those who appropriate water take nothing more or less than the fate of their fellow men and that is why water distribution should not fall into private hands. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy has rightly concluded that access to water is a human right and that water is therefore not a commercial product. the question is how to combat water scarcity and pollution. the relevant polluter-pays principle allows for substantial taxation of the profits of polluting companies but does not justify a considerable increase in household costs. the increase in the quantities of fresh, healthy and potable water available should be achieved through the desalination of seawater and not through new pumping of aquifers or the diversion of rivers to artificial lakes. there was a time when the soviet union wanted to fill the aral sea with water from rivers flowing to the far north. today, spain wants to divert half of the flow of the river ebro to develop tourism in the south of the country. all this at the expense of the plants, animals and people living along the current watercourse. thanks to the criticism, the right wing is blocking the project. this shows that money and prestige continue to take precedence over sustainable environmental management.

in writing. -{nl) the imagination with which packaging is designed nowadays is a form of advertising designed to attract buyers. this practice leads to a significant waste of material. it seems ecological to blame the consumer who buys packaged food or other consumer products. these consumers do not produce this waste, which they receive through their purchases. they become victims of a paired sale because it is now impossible, in many cases, to buy a product without the waste it contains. that is why we must fight directly the production and purchase of waste, not the consumers. it is therefore right that mrs corbey, in the proposed resolution, holds manufacturers and sellers responsible for the prevention of packaging waste, while noting that the 1994 packaging directive has not produced any conclusive results. the european commission is refraining from making new proposals and member states are discussing recycling with years of delay. the rapporteur's proposal is still too much in the balance between two possibilities. i wholeheartedly support his attempt to prevent waste. i am opposed to the consumer paying for all this waste. recycling is important, but it is not the main solution.

the rapporteur. - thank you again, and for the broad support for the proposals. this may be a pyrrhic victory, but we'll see. i wanted to raise the following point. we have here a document on the rights of employees in the event of insolvency, i.e. when a company is unable to meet its financial obligations. it is a revision of council directive 80/987eec with a number of improvements compared to what was previously contained therein. such a directive is intended to provide a minimum of protection in the event of insolvency. at almost the same time as i was appointed rapporteur on this dossier, a group of people came in from the company sintel in spain - a company that had been spun off from telefonica, sold, actually - who had been protesting in madrid for months because they had not been paid their salaries for months. in other words, i did not need a more realistic description beyond what i already knew at the time to make the report behind the insolvency terminology feel viable. the old document is of course from 1980. a lot has changed in the meantime, particularly in the labour markets, in terms of the types of workers and their definitions, there is more globalisation and internationalisation of the economy, there are more companies operating both in a particular country and outside it. there are also cases where it is not clear which country is actually responsible for providing benefits from its fund. there have of course been a number of cases before the court of justice and all of these cases together have led to the commission having to come up with a proposal to amend the existing directive. the three main problems at the time were: the concept of insolvency, the setting of time limits for the guarantee scheme and, in particular, insolvency of a cross-border nature. i have great appreciation for those who have made the commission's proposals and who have also, after extensive consultation, made some amendments. these relate mainly to the new legal basis following the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, the clarification of the scope of application and the possible abolition of the annexes which list a number of groups which may or may not be excluded, the new definition of the concept of intervention and, above all, the new provisions establishing the guarantee fund responsible for crossborder cases. i think it is important to look again at what i describe as the scope of the whole, because there is still a debate about which categories can be excluded, especially in the area of domestic workers and the so-called share fishermen. i would like to see that deleted altogether, as i said in the debate. i think the commission is actually in favour of this, but there are exceptions in some countries and we do not want to make it too difficult. what we do find important is that the commission has now incorporated into these intervention directives, through existing directives, a number of elements which were already developing on that labour market, particularly as regards parttime workers, people working in temporary employment agencies or people with temporary contracts. as we are not yet sure of the consequences of this, we must point out - and many have done so, and this will be discussed in a moment - that there are now more and more categories of selfemployed, semi-selfemployed, quasi-selfemployed as they are called by some, without staff, with staff who may or may not be eligible, and especially those without staff. with staff, they're actually employers. and then we have categories like homeworkers, and note the translation in this case, so i mean literally homeworkers, and so there's a lot of discussion that can be had. it would also be very useful to take a step forward in the legislative work, in line with the discussions in the social dialogue on the modernisation of industrial relations, and that is why we have put forward a number of proposals which are now before you. i therefore ask my colleagues to support amendments concerning the selfemployed, in order to at least open the debate with the council. i would point out that this is a codecision procedure and that after the second reading we will negotiate with each other in order to make a step forward in the field of social security and social policy in europe.

- the convention marks the beginning of a new european constitution, of a bold vision for the future of europe, of a euro which is not monetarily isolated but embedded in socioeconomic policy, of a european commission which transforms itself into a european government, of european elections with european lists and with list drawers who can provide a president for the european commission through the european parliament. we want more qualified majority voting in the council, we want more codecision in the european parliament. the council's meetings should be open to the public so that national parliaments can exercise adequate control over the ministers in the council. we hope for intensive cooperation between the european parliament and the national parliaments. that's vision and future. the convention should be a consensus and not a free catalogue. the convention must engage in an open dialogue with civil society, because part of europe's future lies in increased european cooperation in those areas where citizens expect cross-border results, such as food security, immigration, environmental pollution, international crime and terrorism. but an equal share of policy areas can be left to the regions and civil society. i am therefore in favour of more positive subsidiarity. we must avoid a situation of european autism by concentrating on a renewal of institutional design that goes hand in hand with substantive cooperation. the creation of new forms of european governance means a more open approach and a focus on results. we are achieving this with new instruments such as co- and self-regulation and open coordination, but in doing so we must be sure that, in the event of failure, we have a call-back mechanism to which we can fall back. i am satisfied with the resolutions before us. let us, as the european parliament, vote today for a new, clear form of european governance and let us vote in favour of the convention so that the future of europe can be democratic.
- mr president, important steps have already been taken under the belgian presidency to prepare for the enlargement of the union. the optimism of those involved is even striking: the mention of the date 2004 suggests that the work is almost done. in fact, there is talk of a big bang of ten countries simultaneously. commissioner verheugen is so wise to talk about up to ten new countries possibly joining in 2004. it is not for us to set an accession date for the applicant countries: the 2004 is an assumption and a lot, but it does not guarantee anything for any member state. so let us and they do not cease to do our utmost to achieve a good and credible result. within the present union, much work remains to be done to explain the meaning of enlargement. of course, many are rightly very excited about this marvelous, historic process. but under the influence of those who think they can make political money out of xenophobic feelings, a climate of hesitation has arisen. false representations about the cost of enlargement are circulating. they are meant to evoke fear and are based on so-called worst-case scenarios: it is not as if it has not been clear for some time that this whole enlargement process is taking place, in terms of costs, below the financial horizon of the eu budget. the european union is not a political union, but a political union. that was made clearer than ever by the events of september 11. the fight against serious crime and terrorism is a common concern and any reticence in this area will threaten the security of citizens. it is indeed extremely strange that our legal union as such has not led to greater trust between member states in each other's legal systems. a great deal of work will have to be done in the coming period.
- mr president, the forthcoming laeken summit will be a very important meeting: the european council will have to decide on the agenda for the convention which will make the proposals for reform of the european institutions, and everyone knows how important agendas are for the outcome of consultations. we are satisfied with the planned composition of the convention, although i note that there must be a political balance. the national parliaments will have to pay particular attention to this. i also believe that the president of the convention should be elected by the convention itself. as regards the agenda for the 2003-04 igc, the council has of course the four points of declaration 23 to the treaty of nice. i would like to say briefly the following about these four points. as regards the division of powers, we are in favour of a more federal structure of the european union with a clear division of tasks between the union, the member states and the regions. as regards the structure of future treaties, we are in favour of a basic constitutional treaty which should also include the charter. as regards the role of the national parliaments, we believe that they should in particular direct and control their own ministers to ensure that european policies are implemented. are there any other themes for the convention? - i know! i would like to mention five of them briefly. the common foreign and security policy must be included in the community pillar. the police and judicial policy and the criminal justice policy must also be community-oriented, with a european public prosecutor's office, a european public prosecutor and a community europol. the european parliament should be given full legislative and budgetary powers. the president of the european commission should be elected by the european parliament and the european council of ministers should meet in public when it is about legislation. i am glad that mr prodi has now said that and i am very curious whether mr michel shares that view. these are the issues which are particularly relevant to transparency and the democratic nature of the union and which, in my view, should be included on the agenda of the convention, so that the union, when the new member states join, will have a stronger foundation which meets the requirements of a modern state governed by the rule of law.

- following the attacks of 11 september, europe also needed to strengthen its anti-terrorism policy. the commission's proposal on the definition and penalties of terrorist acts therefore deserves support. less enthusiastic is the commission's proposal for a european arrest warrant with a general scope, and with the abolition of the requirement of double criminality across the board. that's a bridge too far for several reasons: it forces countries with milder criminal justice systems on the defensive and raises questions about due process. the general scope of the proposal no longer relates to the fight against terrorism. there is therefore no basis for the enormous political pressure and the breath-taking pace of decision-making. such a proposal represents a revolution in the application of national and european criminal law and therefore deserves a well-considered and transparent decision-making process, preceded by a proper public debate. the commission has already proposed that the council should be consulted on the proposal, and parliament is forced to give its opinion on the commission proposal when the council has already done so. a positive list instead of a negative one, and that behind closed doors. it is to be hoped and expected that the discussion in the council will eventually lead to an acceptable compromise, but we do not know that yet and we will not vote on that tomorrow. the debate in this house and the vote in this form and at this moment are therefore a little absurd and, in fact, premature. for this reason, the dutch pvda delegations will abstain tomorrow from voting on the commission's proposal for a european arrest warrant.
- mr president, my group would naturally like to help in the rapid establishment of common rules on civil aviation safety: it is not necessary to explain this further after the events of 9/11. we are concerned with the four points which we have set out in our amendments, in which we want to take account of the interests of the sector, in which safety and a fair distribution of the burdens and costs associated with it must be paramount. firstly, we must strive for the highest possible level of security when it comes to the protection of airports and airports. that is the least the citizens can ask of us. point two: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used effectively. that means we have to look carefully at whether what is proposed will work in practice. the third point is that the commission, in cooperation with ecac and icao, should determine whether airports in third countries, i.e. airports outside the scope of the regulation, meet essential safety requirements, as any leaks in the new system will mainly arise there. i know from personal experience how to get on a plane in albania without going through bomb-screening. the fourth and final point is that we want to see uniform rules for the financing of the proposed measures in order to avoid unfair competition. this may involve state aid, but it is directly related to the additional costs associated with the scheme in question. of course, this must be demonstrated by the need for the aid. the sector itself, operators and users, must also bear part of the costs.

mr president, the conclusion of an association agreement between the european community and its member states and egypt gives rise to very mixed feelings. my concern is particularly directed at the unequal and insecure social position of egyptian christians. the oral question to the commission underlines this concern. how does it intend to persuade the egyptian authorities to improve the situation of the coptic community? please note, we are talking about at least six million egyptian citizens. it is therefore particularly regrettable that the very violation of their fundamental rights is not explicitly mentioned in the motion for a resolution. to illustrate, let me mention three serious abuses that egyptian christians suffered: not only are the egyptian authorities blocking the construction of new churches, they are also complicit in the criminal prosecution of muslims who want to become christians. the latter is done under the cloak of subversive activity. thirdly, there is legal uncertainty among the christian community in upper egypt: it is exposed to outright religious persecution by muslim fundamentalists. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european parliament is able to exercise its right of initiative in the matter. i therefore ask the commission, the council and the governments of the member states to take these abuses into account in their discussions with the egyptian authorities. they are obliged to do so by virtue of the terms of this association agreement. the positive fact that since september 11 the coptic churches have been in dialogue with the egyptian government reinforces this essential provision.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. when the commission first put forward its proposal a month or two ago, there was some doubt. that doubt had nothing to do with the foreign affairs committee's assessment of the reconstruction agency: the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. this positive evaluation was recently confirmed by a very complimentary remark from the court of auditors on the rapid and efficient way in which the office has carried out its work so far. so our initial doubts had nothing to do with the bureau but stemmed from the fact that the commission itself did not seem to know exactly where it wanted to go with aid in the balkans. should it be run entirely through the office for reconstruction, first in yugoslavia, then in macedonia and perhaps in albania and croatia in the future, or would the commission stick to its original policy of decentralising powers to the representations in the various countries? we have now had the opportunity to speak to the commissioner about this. he promised that the commission would soon, early next year, come forward with a position on the strategy to be followed in relation to aid in the balkans, and that in doing so it would specify the role of the reconstruction office and the role of representation in a decentralised form. we'll be waiting for that report with interest. at the moment - and that removes the doubt - there is no alternative to the agency playing an important role if we are to provide aid in macedonia quickly and efficiently. i think we are in complete agreement with the commission on this point. why is it so important to provide aid in macedonia now, and to do so through the agency? i have already stressed many times, both earlier in this debate and on other occasions, particularly after 11 september, the great importance of the developments in macedonia for the european union. the importance of macedonia is many times greater than that of the relatively small country in the balkans. it is the first time that the european union has managed to do, with one voice, in an adequate way in the balkans, in macedonia, what we might have wanted to see happen there for a long time. it is the greatest success of european foreign policy to date. speak with one voice and do what you're good at: that is what the commission and the european union have done in macedonia so far. there have been talks and consultations, compromises have been made, financial aid has been promised and limited military aid has been promised. i believe that this is the best the european union can do at the moment, and it is important that this effort - - mr president, it is disappointing that we have only now been able to deal with the very important report of the temporary committee on human genetics. the fiori report provides an ethical framework won't be for another decade or two. but the wonderful therapies that can be developed using stem cells, shouldn't we develop and use them? i think so, but again, not at the expense of human embryos. so it's a miracle, and i consider it a blessing from god, that there are also adult stem cells. these stem cells, found in umbilical cord, blood, adipose tissue, and brain tissue, among other things, - mr president, the matter we are dealing with today has received a great deal of attention. we've heard from many experts, visited many. we have consulted with our fellow parliamentarians at home and abroad, from the eu member states as well as from the acceding countries. there have been many discussions and after all this input, mr president, i have formed a very personal opinion on this difficult but also ethically charged matter. i would like to say that i do respect any judgment that has been made in good faith. left or right, conservative or modern, is not the issue here. i cannot therefore allow my position or that of other members to be labelled as fundamentalist, as has just happened. mr president, my views and voting patterns are largely in line with what has been agreed in the group. i disagree on one point: i'm all for using surplus embryos from ivf, but i want to deliberately create extra embryos in containers. i am against blocking the possibilities that therapeutic cloning may offer in the future to cure diseases like parkinson's and alzheimer's. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. i reject the production of embryos for research purposes only. i think we're dealing with a definitional problem here in therapeutic cloning. may a nucleus from an egg cell of mine, combined with a skin cell of mine, serve to make a heart cell of mine sometime in the future? in conclusion, mr president, the patent law is not good: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european patent system is not disrupted by the introduction of new technologies. i therefore ask my d66 and vvd colleagues who voted differently when the report was being considered to support our group on this point too.
mr president, the debate we are having today is of great importance. after all, we're talking about nothing less than life itself. we're talking about scientific research that has the potential to cure serious human diseases, such as parkinson's, alzheimer's, ms, diabetes and perhaps even aids, or to improve or extend life. this is not a matter to be treated lightly. it is therefore a bad thing when this parliament explicitly refuses to recognise the distinction between reproductive and therapeutic cloning: the first is focused on creating new people, the second on creating new tissue. to prohibit the second directly or indirectly is to close your eyes to a lot of scientific possibilities that could help people. the report is far from being subsidiary. it is precisely ethical and moral dilemmas that must be resolved as closely as possible to the people themselves, since they directly appeal to the individual conscience. the call to the commission to come up with legislation cannot therefore be without the approval of my group. finally, i am sorry to be disturbed by the monopoly which some of my colleagues on the right and the greens believe they have in the field of ethics. some colleagues give the impression that the most restrictive position is automatically the most ethically high-minded. if we make promising research more difficult or even prohibit it, research which could bring a cure or alleviate suffering for sick people or even save their lives, then that too is a decision with grave ethical implications.
- mr president, many people still suffer from incurable degenerative diseases affecting the whole body, such as multiple sclerosis, parkinson's, alzheimer's, diabetes and leukaemia. others have, in an otherwise healthy body, malfunctioning or damaged vital organs, such as the heart, kidneys, liver, or lungs. as humans, we have succeeded in changing all things in the world outside of ourselves, but we can still only solve our own physical defects to a limited extent. we also find repairing and improving our physical quality to be downright creepy. is man going to act as his own creator and is that contrary to the purpose for which humans were put on earth? few will feel for creating invulnerable superhumans who will eventually supplant normal humans. moreover, sacrificing human life to give a better quality of life to others evokes feelings of cannibalism. sometimes the discussion is about extremes. the first extreme is that of banning all scientific research and imprisoning researchers, the second is that of allowing all commercial applications, such as those developed by the american company advanced cell technology, and thus making possible on an individual level everything that rich people can and want to pay for. i reject both extremes. the use of stem cells from one's own body or, if necessary, from residual embryos is justifiable. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's research programmes are not disrupted by the introduction of new technologies. the same is true of valuing and adjusting human life at the insurers' request. i am more comfortable with mr caudron's line than with mr fiori's.
- mr president, this debate is about much more than our view of human genetics: it is also a question of the role we as european politicians assume in the assessment of ethics, science and the integrity of the european citizen. i'm not sure i'm the right man for the job, and i think our humility is in order. citizens are very well able to make their own decisions in good conscience. i am personally in favour of scientific research being as free as possible with the possible prospect of curing diseases which are so far incurable such as parkinson's, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, although in the latter case you can of course also simply stop smoking. the work of our committee has shown that european science is conscientious in its responsibility. i cannot in good conscience accept that we do not support or even prohibit the research that is being proposed, including therapeutic cloning and stem cell research using embryonic remains. of course, others will come to a different conclusion and i respect that, but we must also take into account that different member states will come to different legislation. i therefore cannot agree with the proposal before us, mr president, if it remains unchanged.
- mr president, the ethical dimension of this debate is crucial, but we must not leave it there: we also need to talk about power. who has control over the human body? the bio-patent directive regulates that power. unfortunately, this directive is not entirely clear. the possibilities for patents are too broadly defined and this places too much power in the hands of the large patent holders. we have to counter that. firstly, we must subject the directive to a thorough evaluation of its socioeconomic implications and propose a revision if necessary. secondly, we must ensure that pharmaceutical companies are in touch with the public. there has to be public influence on an investigative agenda. what do we want to know, what can we know and who can know what? thirdly, we must ensure that gene therapy remains accessible to all. the cost of gene therapy is very high for the time being and this may compromise its accessibility. fourthly, we must ask ourselves what the social consequences of the medical revolution are: we're getting older, we're getting more individual, we're eliminating abnormalities, and all of that has implications for human relationships, for the labor market, for health care. finally, we need to set up a public research agenda that we don't have to be bound by artificial, ethical boundaries. we need to move from a narrow, orthodox religion-based ethics to a broad social ethics. the sixth framework programme plays a key role in this, but cooperation between national public institutions is at least as important.

in writing. - (nl) as labour is a major cost factor in the production of goods, and even more so in the provision of services, it is increasingly seen that employers are trying to reduce their payment obligations. and sometimes, when employers are unfair or in trouble, they try to avoid paying wages. the employees do not receive their pay or do not receive it until after the judge intervenes. the european commission proposal fails to define the cases where there is a question of an employer, an employee or a pay due. the rapporteur, mr bouwman, rightly proposes that this regulation be extended to small independent contractors, homeworkers and domestic workers, so that there is no escape for a malicious employer who stops paying wages. the establishment of national guarantee funds becomes mandatory, and these must remain separate from the operating capital of employers. all wage agreements of employees - including overtime pay, holiday pay and severance pay - must be covered by this fund and no ceiling can be set for payments. it is one of the best proposals of the european union, which finally does something for the employees. in recent years, most of the proposals have served the interests of employers above all.
in writing. - (nl) the growth of air traffic had already stopped before planes full of unsuspecting passengers were used by terrorists as missiles to destroy tall buildings. several years of fierce competition between the good old domestic airlines and the new adventurers in the market have resulted in overcapacity which has left airlines unable to cope with the downturns of fortune and led them to beg for public subsidies to survive. the choice now seems to be between a dry run, with a series of airline bankruptcies and mass redundancies, and price competition subsidised by the public authorities, which will keep overcapacity in place. if mrs. foster gets what she wants, taxpayers can wipe out the deficit of privatized corporations and private companies will have a say in public policy. i am advocating a solution other than dry cleaning or subsidies. the point is that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the basis of the information it has received from the member states. the costs of insurance, security, advertising campaigns and the tax on kerosene have to be fully integrated into the price of the flight, so that the plane loses its competitive advantage over the train. the re-training and the security of life of the staff will then be able to be financed in the short term by the new tax revenue, without having to subsidize the companies again.

in writing. - (nl) i support the report under consideration and the proposal for a framework decision on the fight against terrorism. as terrorism is largely transnational, european countries will have to work together. on the other hand, the european arrest warrant goes too far in one respect. this is the negative list and the removal of the double criminality proposed by the commission. as member states are already slow to hand over criminals, a general arrest warrant and the elimination of double incrimination that it entails will face major problems. several member states, including the netherlands, will do everything in their power to avoid extradition for, for example, cases of euthanasia or abortion. that is why i supported the amendments tabled by my colleagues niall andrews and brian crowley. they are in favour of a positive list, which also corresponds to the council's present position. the european arrest warrant will then only apply to the crimes on this list. i am thinking here of an arrest warrant which will apply to criminal offences for which the criminal law has already been harmonised at european level, such as terrorism. if this seems to be working well, the number of crimes on the positive list could always be increased. in the future, we may be able to come to a negative list, but it is still too early. it should be borne in mind that the criminal law of the member states is to a large extent linked to national culture. at the moment, the differences between member states are simply too great. since the amendments by mr andrews and mr crowley have not been taken up, we cannot support the second part of mr watson's report on the european arrest warrant. we do not think it would be wise to vote for a negative list when the council has agreed on a positive list.

in writing. - (nl) mr president, i voted against the watson report for the following reasons. i fully support measures against terrorism and i believe that in this area eu member states have the possibility and the need to work closely together. the european arrest warrant can make an important contribution to the effectiveness of the fight against terrorism in the european territory. i think a european arrest warrant is desirable. however, it must be better designed and better weighed so as not to interfere with other important matters. the draft under consideration does not offer sufficient safeguards and is likely to undermine the liberal criminal policy of the netherlands. in order to reach a compromise, i tried, through the rapporteur, to table an amendment which sets the following condition for the exercise of the european arrest warrant: the european arrest warrant can only be used for crimes committed in the territory of the requesting state. however, this amendment was blocked by the socialists in the working party. i also voted against the report because another draft should be adopted by the council. i am therefore in favour of anti-terrorism measures, including a european arrest warrant, but not at the expense of the liberal criminal policy of the netherlands.
in writing. - (nl) there is a great deal of confusion about the phenomenon of terrorism. most terrorists do not choose to be terrorists but feel compelled, due to the misunderstanding of their role as opposition by political leaders and their conflicting views, to resort to extreme and unacceptable means which they consider to be their last resort. some leaders who later became respectable, such as those in israel, palestine, south africa and many former colonies, began their political careers as terrorists. the fight against terrorism is not fought by creating more misunderstanding and mistrust, but by ensuring that the problems to which terrorists want to draw our attention are solved quickly and without violence. political leaders who see the danger of terrorism everywhere risk finding themselves in a police state where basic freedoms and democratic rights are absent. this leads to a deterioration of the political climate which feeds the mill of terrorism. law-abiding citizens are no longer protected from arbitrary arrests, long-term pre-trial detention and controversial extraditions. the same applies when non-terrorist opponents are intimidated or when people can be imprisoned for acts that are not punishable in their country. as long as there are no sufficient guarantees to prevent these phenomena, i believe that european regulation will hinder rather than promote the fight against terrorism.

in writing. - (nl) the fisheries agreements concluded by the eu with developing countries are harmful both to the environment and to these countries. the fact that eu fishermen are visibly feeling the pressure to move their activities to non-eu waters shows that the fish population in eu waters has been so reduced by these activities that there is now insufficient revenue. the environmental problem must be tackled at its source, by reducing the capacity of the fleet, not by going fishing elsewhere. in addition, these agreements are also detrimental to local economies as modern eu vessels deprive local fishermen of their catch. it is absurd that the eu should be paying money to the governments of these countries to help these fishermen find another way of making a living. the amendments proposed by the committee on fisheries and the eldr group to the commission proposal constitute an improvement to the text of the agreement. d66 therefore supported these amendments. since we oppose the agreement in its present form for the reasons stated above, we voted against the legislative resolution.
in writing. - (nl) for years, the quality and public health of food production have been subordinated to lower production costs. a cheap food assortment was to keep the cost affordable for the masses. both public authorities and private companies agreed that cost reduction was necessary and was achieved by increasing scale, using artificial ingredients, intensifying the use of space, importing third world animal feed and drastically reducing human labour. for the same reason, some have fed the animals with poisoned meat or grass, or have crammed the animals into cages or trucks, a practice that facilitates the spread of disease. those who wanted better quality food had to turn to a separate distribution system for the higher-paid people. it was only when people were found to be suffering from incurable diseases caused by contaminated food that more and more people became concerned about what they were eating. once again, accidents had to happen before a real solution was found. the solution is not to burden the european bureaucracy or to quarrel over the seat and direction of a new institution. food security can only exist if we stop putting cost and profit above everything else and create maximum transparency in complaints, minority opinions, composition and safety measures. i hope that the revolutionary development described by mr staes will take place, but it has yet to prove its existence.

in writing. - (nl) in the past, small businesses were numerous. in the last half century, they have been systematically bought up or swept away by new, larger competitors. interest in small business has only been revived in recent years. unlike in the past, the big companies are interested in this because they can get rid of activities that they are not able to provide at such a competitive price. they employ outsiders operating in countries where wages are lower or sell vulnerable departments of their company to staff or management. thus, the risks incurred by the company, such as absorbing high or low points in the transport sector or in the repair sector, are shifted to others. collective agreements or regulations aimed at improving working conditions, which are so onerous, are also losing much of their relevance. people working in these small firms, if they want to survive, are forced to work longer and longer hours than they did in the big ones. the small ones believe they are independent, when in reality they are at the mercy of the banking sector and the large companies with which they have contracts. their very existence may be called into question overnight. it is likely that public support for small enterprises will ultimately benefit the larger ones. i do not, however, reject this aid without some form of legal action, because there are also situations where small businesses create significant new opportunities for certain categories of workers, in particular immigrants and pioneers who bring technical innovations to the market.

budgetary method and it is true that this method always leads to an agreement in the end, but the annual budgetary dance is still a somewhat irrational process. the commission makes a proposal, the council takes a lot of money off it, parliament throws in a few extra ones and then we have to make do with it in the famous consultation. i have toyed with the idea of interrupting the dance and simply leaving a number of council discounts under heading 5, for example the discounts at the court of justice. i think it would be a good idea to confront the council with the consequences of its actions and its unilateral obsession to remain well below the ceiling of the financial perspective. i'm sorry i didn't do it, but i did. i hear the comments, you should have. i didn't do it because otherwise the wrong people would be affected. this idea of taking responsibility is in line with the idea we also raised in the first reading, namely that political promises by heads of government and ministers must be accompanied by a financial picture. we have gained the necessary experience in the reconstruction of the balkans and it seems to me that it is more just and fair to say whether new tasks require new money - and that is also a promise - or whether, for example, aid to a crisis area requires a discount on peace projects in the middle east or on projects against sexual violence in south africa. the advantage, in any case, is that aid to afghanistan has been a prominent part of the consultations this time and, unlike in the case of the balkans, external pledges were not made first at donor conferences, after which we could put the patches on, but were discussed in the consultations. i hope that this was not a matter of timing but the beginning of a favourable development. another bizarre aspect of the budgetary procedure is the implementation of the budget and we as a parliament are also guilty of empty promises. we want tens of millions more for south america, for example, without knowing exactly why only 60% of last year's money was spent. and every year we again resolve - and that is no reason not to do so this year - to monitor better and also to adjust the in writing. - (nl) in the absence of democratic regulation by the authorities, health becomes a commodity. this makes the commodity accessible to the rich and powerful, while it is lacking for the poor and powerless. we find that the life expectancy of disadvantaged population groups is shorter than that of the more advantaged groups. there is a constant and significant push to replace income-based insurance premiums with a single premium for all, regardless of income. commercial companies offer special care to those who can afford it and are willing to pay. hospitals are entering the commercial market, where the wealthiest can get ahead of the curve, while loss-making treatments are eliminated. waiting lists are getting longer, people are being sent to remote hospitals in other member states and the rate of preventable deaths is increasing. to counter this trend, it is imperative that the authorities ensure that there is quality health care available to all. a european community action programme in the field of public health can help. the amendments rejected after the first reading must now be supported by a large majority, in order to make it clear that health is not a commodity subject to financial compromise and that the public health sector in many of the applicant countries needs to be improved after 12 years of neglect.

commission. – even before the rise to power of the taliban in afghanistan during 1995-1996 the eu was conscious of the poor position and status of women in afghan society. this was recognised in the nature of the aid programmes which we financed at that time and which had a strong focus on the provision of health care, education and employment creation for women. with the arrival in power of the taliban in kabul in 1996, the eu agreed a common position on afghanistan. the common position is renewed annually and clearly sets out among its objectives the promotion of respect for international law and human rights, including the rights of women and children. in addition, the eu undertakes in the common position to support aid programmes which integrate gender concerns and actively attempt to promote the equitable participation of both men and women and promote peace and human rights. as a result, the commission, through its echo-financed programmes and through its budget for aid to uprooted people, continued, even during the taliban period, to finance actions which provided health care and education for women and girls and provided employment opportunities and training for women. i met many of these women and men in kabul last week. it made me start talking about what i call the 'other afghanistan'. we all know the afghanistan of the warlords. but there is an alternative afghanistan. we also have heroes and heroines of peace and compassion. many of them work in projects that we are funding, did so during the taliban regime and have continued doing so since september 11. in an echo-funded project for vulnerable children, i met the girls sitting there learning to read and write and asked how many wanted to become housewives when they grew up. only a few hands were somewhat hesitantly raised. then i asked how many wanted to become schoolteachers or doctors. everyone put their hand up – they all wanted to do something. a very nice moment i would say, and their lady teacher was proud. another project involved a woman producing quilts which we use for refugee projects. she was alone, her husband had died in the conflict, and when the taliban came to power, she had to stop working as a crane operator in the construction industry. she has 10 children and her home was being used. they sat on the floor sewing these quilts and that was a very nice experience. at the end, when we left, i could not resist giving her a hug to express my feelings – clearly not politically correct when the neighbours could see or, indeed, at all. but it was well received, and i was quite happy to be part of a civilised and nice meeting of cultures in the centre of kabul. now we are fortunately in the post-taliban era. changes are now possible and we hope that what was achieved in bonn on december 5 will pave the way for a big improvement in the situation of women and girls in the country. women were included in the delegations in bonn; women will hold office in the interim administration. the provisional agreement makes a number of specific references to the guaranteed participation of women in the next phases of the political process – the loya jirga and the transitional administration. all of this will be overseen by the un which has a constitutional role, recognised in the provisional agreement, to monitor the conduct of the interim authority and the emergency loya jirga, as well as providing for the development and implementation of a programme of human rights education to promote respect for and understanding of human rights in afghanistan. the commission is currently processing new, additional aid programmes worth eur 28.5 million, which will start being implemented in the coming weeks, for emergency aid and aid to uprooted people. gender will, of course, be either a specific or horizontal issue in all of these programmes. echo is already present in kabul and we will formally inaugurate the echo office there in the middle of january. commission officials plan to start being there permanently from 1 february 2002. it is therefore important to ensure follow-up also in view of what we are discussing here. progress will provide crucial indicators to allow the eu and the rest of the international community to judge the commitment of the new afghan administration to the engagement that they now have entered into. i must warn you not to expect miracles. it is a very traditional society, especially outside kabul. the reality on the ground does not reflect the elite in kabul that we easily get in touch with. there are many deep-seated differences. we must take a very broad-based approach and make sure that we deliberately include women in the many decentralised activities that we carry out across the country.

conflict in ambon on 19 january 1999, the day before the islamic holiday of idul fitr, the laskar jihad have killed at least 10,000 christians and displaced scores of others in fear of their lives. i am extremely concerned that after the moluccas, this anti-christian power has now also been blown to sulawesi. i am reminded, mr president, of the story of the christian boy of eight, which was documented in the autumn of this year. the little boy was on the bus with his mother. on the way, about 50 muslim terrorists forced the vehicle to stop. the robbers checked the passengers for religious identity. two turned out to be christians, the woman and her son. with brutal force, they dragged the boy off the bus, leaving the mother in a state of total confusion. no matter how loudly the victim screamed in his terror, it was not to his advantage. the terrorists dragged him across the tarmac into the jungle, and the boy was never heard from again. one of the many documented laskar jihad bus robberies in sulawesi. mr president, i ask the council and the commission to do everything in their power to help fight terrorism in indonesia, to consider how they can support a process of conciliation on the ground and to consider what measures they can take to promote economic development in this region.
- mr president, on indonesia, timor and the moluccas, we in parliament have adopted a number of important resolutions. when we talk about indonesia, we are talking about a world empire in which - actually under dictatorship - whole sections of the population have been forcibly transported to other parts of the world empire, the transmigration. that is still the root of many complex conflicts in that world empire. at the same time, it's a huge step to move from dictatorship to democracy. since 1999 there has been talk of democratization, but it is extremely difficult: on the one hand, there are efforts to strengthen democracy, on the other hand, there are violent ethnic conflicts in many areas. jihad, which was previously active in the moluccas, is now active in sulawesi. theys hiyo eluay was murdered in papua. and time and again it appears that the military has difficulty in really breaking away and really accepting the rule of law and democracy. that's very clear in papua: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to support the development of the regions concerned. we must therefore strongly condemn the murder committed and do everything to make this process of reconciliation possible. the same is true of sulawesi. let us therefore renounce the terrorists, the jihadists, and at the same time support the indonesian authorities. the vast majority of the population wants reconciliation, wants to live together, wants to build society together. ordinary citizens, whether they are christian or muslim, have no need for jihad. and that is why we, with all our experience, have an important role to play in this respect, in all modesty.
- mr president, after a period of relative calm in indonesia, we have been shocked again since november by serious violence in sulawesi and celebes, among other places, and by the murder of theys hiyo eluay, leader of the papuans in irian jaya. i should like to say a few words about the murder of theys hiyo eluay, which took place on 10 november after he had held a meeting on behalf of the papuan community with the leadership of the indonesian military unit in west papua. theys hiyo eluay was not only a charismatic leader of the papuans, he was also a moderate man, who did not seek total independence for his province but sought autonomy within the indonesian state and had succeeded in obtaining this autonomy through the government and through the indonesian parliament. in october, the indonesian parliament ratified the autonomy and after a dinner with the regional military staff, he was assassinated on the evening of november 10. it is a sign of the internal situation in indonesia that military units in the region can frustrate a constructive process of peace and reconciliation in such a way that this kind of murder takes place. many believe it was a revenge action, because an autonomous irian jaya could never give the military the power and financial profit they had before. my request to the commission and the council is that they ask the indonesian government to investigate this murder to the bottom and to punish the perpetrators, so that justice is done in an area where injustice prevails. i also ask for help for the regional government in irian jaya, for example in setting up a management academy, so that people can really see themselves as having the chance to run that region. and now, chairman, the situation in sulawesi and celebes. it is the same laskar jihad groups that have already caused so much misery in the moluccas, causing thousands of deaths and hundreds of thousands of refugees. in this connection too, we call on the commission and the council to ask the indonesian government to protect the christian community in indonesia and to better control the fundamentalist muslim groups. president. - if indonesia is to maintain its respectable and important position, the present government must put a stop to this violence and the european union must make it clear to indonesia that political killings and violence against religious minorities are not acceptable, otherwise the relationship between the european union and indonesia will be put under pressure in my view.
- mr president, it is more than ten years since aung san suu kyi, the president of burma elected by 80% of the population, was awarded both the nobel prize and the sakharov prize for her peaceful protest against the military coup and military dictatorship in her country. for the past ten years, she has been living permanently either in prison or under house arrest while her country has been transformed into one of the most violent countries in the world. more than half of the members of parliament have fled, been imprisoned, expelled or killed, and several million burmese have fled to india, bangladesh, thailand, malaysia, the united states and europe. in burma there is a massive repression of members of the party of mrs aung san suu kyi and members of minority groups. there is also forced labour in the construction of infrastructure and burma is now the second largest drug exporter in the world after bolivia. this military dictatorship is fuelled by drugs, by forced and cheap labour, by terror and violence, and this situation has lasted for more than ten years. our question is again: the european commission, put a stop to investment or an economic boycott on this country, as the united states has done in the meantime. it is perhaps the best punishment for this violent dictatorship and the best gift you can give to the elected president of burma, mrs aung san suu kyi. president. - i also offer my condolences to leyla zana. it is not right that a country which wants to join the european union should delay such a question for so long. let turkey also show that it wants to be a state governed by the rule of law and to give leyla zana a full seat in her country and in the parliament in which she was elected as soon as possible.
- madam president, i have a question on the full minutes of the meetings: last wednesday evening vice-president onesta announced that an urgent debate on the european arrest warrant would be voted on thursday morning. on thursday morning, however, mr watson, chairman of the committee on civil liberties, asked the house to vote on an urgent debate on - and i quote from the full report - 'two framework decisions from the council, one on combating terrorism, the other on a proposal for a european arrest warrant'. confusion everywhere. it also shows above all that the decision of last thursday was taken in a very hasty and careless manner. mr president, can you tell me, on the basis of the full minutes of the meetings, on what specific subjects we are going to have an urgent debate? and while we are in the process of clarifying this, can you assure me that the text on the european arrest warrant, which we were able to amend until 4 p.m. last thursday, is still the same text and that it has not been changed over the weekend? if that were the case, we would be making ourselves the laughing stock of immortality again today.
- mr president, there are many questions in the laeken declaration: the european union is a political union, a political union of the people, a political union of the people. the new convention cannot, of course, answer all these questions. i therefore believe that improving transparency and a clear division of powers between the european union and the member states should be given priority. i was pleasantly surprised by the way the questions were worded on this last point. it is clear that there are no taboos if one dares to question even the surreptitious transfer of powers to brussels. i was also surprised, though not positively, by the composition of the convention's bureau: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. what role remains for the ordinary convention member? not much of a role, i'm afraid. but that threatens the quality of the proposals that this body makes. the convention must be of quality, mr president, if its ideas are not to be shoved into the desks.
- mr president, after 11 september we have succeeded in reducing the freedom of movement of terrorists by means of a number of effective european measures. at the same time, we have realised that the security we are promoting is partial security and that we are essentially addressing a deeper, more fundamental issue, namely the great inequality in this world that is often a breeding ground for conflict. if security is not shared security, it has no chance of success. one in five people in this world don't have access to basic education or basic health care. that requires multilateral action. we are now seeing the united states, which in recent months has been acting more multilaterally, acting more unilaterally in recent days by unilaterally withdrawing from the abm treaty and taking a much more unilateral course with regard to a number of other treaties. it is of the utmost importance that we on the european side try to use this grand coalition to exert pressure so that we continue to act multilaterally: of course, investing heavily in new technologies and then having too little money, attention and energy to fight global poverty is ultimately not the most effective path to shared security. the reconstruction of afghanistan requires support, again with europe in the lead, so that not only the military aspect is emphasized, but also shared security is sought through the path of reconstruction. the same is true of the middle east: europe must exert pressure, not being afraid to be present in nato in its own form and organization - the convention will have to find an institutional form for this - but at the same time it must also have the courage to take the path of shared security. and i would have liked to see that fundamental aspect expressed a little more at the laeken summit. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i call on the presidency and the commission to continue to take initiatives in this area in the coming weeks, both in the middle east and in the balkans and afghanistan. we are in the right position. there are tendencies towards unilateralism: we must not be part of that, but we must call on our allies to adopt a multilateral approach and to give europe a central role in that process.
- mr president, for the outside world, particularly in the netherlands, the laeken summit was a meeting of heads of government where there was a lot of bickering. dispute over who should preside over the convention and dispute over who should host which european agency. these two points absolutely dominated the dutch media. but fortunately, something very good and constructive has happened. the european summit has decided on the convention and not only on the presidency and the two vice-presidencies, which i am also pleased about, but also on the tasks assigned to the convention. fortunately, that assignment is very broad. the convention will have to provide a better distribution and definition of the union's competences, will have to consider how the system of union treaties and legislation can be simplified and how more democracy and transparency can be created in the union. and as regards transparency, i can say at the outset that i am in any case in favour of the european council of ministers playing the role of a senate, on the model of the german bundesrat, a council of ministers which meets in public when it is preparing legislation. the european summit also asked the convention to develop an idea of a constitution for the union and to incorporate the charter of fundamental rights. that's a great first package. but i would also like to say that we believe that more is needed. the convention will also have to consider how the second and third pillars can be integrated into community policy. the commission has already done so in the field of migration policy, and the field of internal security policy is the sector which is now growing rapidly at community level in the wake of the tragic events of 11 september. however, foreign and security policy is still intergovernmental and solana's role is almost impossible in the structure of the european union. we want to incorporate that policy and solana should be vice-president of the european commission. finally, mr president, this time the summit has elected a president and two vice-presidents of the convention. the role would be even stronger if the convention itself, on the initiative of the summit, had been able to choose its president. then maybe there was a woman there. as far as we are concerned, mr president, the convention may also come up with the idea of electing the president of the european commission in the future. then it could be done by the european parliament. the belgian presidency has had a number of problems, but the fact that it has been able to bring this convention to the table makes me feel positive about a presidency which has also had a number of problems.
- the debate on the future of europe is being broadened to include members of parliament and is becoming a public debate, thanks in particular to the belgian presidency. that is good, but there is also a very real risk that the convention will take on a babylonian character because it is all-encompassing and all views can be discussed. in their declaration at laeken, the heads of government did not say anything in fine words. they have now submitted the many questions which they themselves have been unable to answer for ten years to a convention which has only a few months to do so. the question is also whether the convention can reduce the gap with the population. the citizens are not interested in the redistribution of power between the institutions. people are more concerned with the content of the decisions than with the level at which they are made. europe is not served by a trench war between federalists and intergovernmentalists. we must step up our cooperation. the community method will then prove to be the only viable option. the ideological battle over the future of europe has only losers. i think that should have been explained by mr laken.
